The *nirvahaṇa-sandhi* (concluding juncture), characterized by the attainment of the fruit of the action and its unification, is indicated in the seventh act.
Therein—the action (*kārya*)— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "tatra—kāryaṃ". The translation reflects this incomplete state.]
It is the operation that brings about great fruits and the like; as it has been said: "The effect is that which accomplishes the result.
And that [is expressed by] "each one of the heads," "when crushed," and so forth.
In the case of the Lord of the Night-stalkers, [the text says] "He made himself the Lord of Laṅkā," and so forth. It is said:
"The attainment of the complete fruit is designated as the arrival of the fruit (*phalāgama*).
Here, "complete" (*samagra*) means accompanied by incidental fruits (*ānuṣaṅgika-phala*). And that—
Dharma consists in the protection of all the worlds, accompanied by intermediate objectives such as the recovery of Sītā, the consecration, and pre-eminence over the world;
through the adherence to these two [aims], there is the [attainment of] the fourteen ancillaries, beginning with the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*).

The mutual connection [of these elements] is the *nirvahaṇa* juncture (*sandhi*). And it is defined as follows: "That is indeed the *nirvahaṇa* where the various matters from the *mukha* and other junctures, which possess the seed (*bīja*) and are scattered according to their respective places, are brought together toward a single purpose. (7)

And this is indicated here by the passage beginning: "Vasiṣṭha consecrates him with mantras; others, however, having performed various forms of ritual salutation, prostrate themselves, touching the ground with their five limbs. (8)
This is because the activities of Vasiṣṭha, Sugrīva, Vibhīṣaṇa, and others are stated to have the sole purpose of bringing about the exaltation of Rāmabhadra. Its constituent parts are:
conciliation (saṃdhi), obstruction (nirodha), connection (grathana), determination (nirṇaya), and consultation (paribhāṣaṇa).
The composition consists of the moments of clarity and bliss within the embrace of the Bhāṣā.
"The conclusion of the previous state, the praise, and [the colophon] make fourteen" (9).
"Tamisra," and so forth.
*mūrcchālāni* means "possessing fainting spells" (*mūrchāvanti*); [the suffix] *lac* is applied because it belongs to the *sidhma* group. *Agadaṅkāraḥ* means "physician";
he possesses the status of a healer (*bhiṣaj*) because of his power to destroy darkness (*timira*). The augment *mum* is applied according to the rule: *kāre satyāgadasya*.
"O progenitor"—this address as a kinsman is intended to express pride in the purity of one's lineage.
"Speech" refers to censure, which serves as the motive for entering the fire; the ablative case is used according to Pāṇini 2.3.42: *vibhāṣā guṇe 'strīyām*.

"Then," meaning immediately after the knowledge of purity; "she went out," meaning she went out having been told, "You are pure. The mention of the proximity of the sun and other celestial bodies is for the purpose of [indicating] them...
Because he is the witness of karma; as it has been said: "The sun and the moon, fire and wind, heaven, earth, water, the heart, and Yama; day and night,"
Both twilights and Dharma know the conduct of a man.
(13) Thus ends the first [chapter].

Regarding the phrase "each one" (*ekaikāni*) and so forth: the word *eka* denotes that which is without a companion (*asahāya*), because if it were intended to refer to a number (*saṃkhyā*), the use of the plural would be untenable.

In the rule *ekād ākiniccāsahāye* (Pāṇini 5.3.52), the form [is derived] by the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *kan*, which is carried over from the preceding rule due to the particle *ca*. Through the process of *ekaśeṣa*—where "one and one and one" becomes *ekāni*—the word *eka* [is formed]. Thereafter, "one..."

The reduplication [of the word *asahāya*] is for the sake of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), and there is the application of the *bahuvrīhi*-like treatment; for this very reason, by the rule "supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ," there is the elision of the nominal suffixes (*sub*). [Thus we have: *asahāyāni śirāṃsi*.
The meaning is "having cut many times.
Even so, although the conclusion [of the cutting] rests upon a single individual instance of a head, [the process is repeated].
Nevertheless, the use of the plural number is justified by the distinction between the various forms of assistance.
Since the oblations other than the *pūrṇāhuti* are generally taken up only once, they are described as being singular. *Tejas* means prowess or majesty.
The *pūrṇāhuti*—so called because it fulfills all deficiencies and excesses—is the final oblation, characterized by the remnants of what has been offered. As it was said by Śiva: "Then..."
"Having indeed filled the *sruva* with the ghee remaining from the oblation (18).
Here, the word "ghee" (*ghṛta*) refers to the substance to be offered. Whatever is excessive, deficient, or even contrary in the oblation—all that [is corrected by this].
"And this is called the *pūrṇāhuti* (the final oblation) here because it fulfills [all desires]. (19) And:
*svastyayana* is that which brings about auspiciousness by means of warding off misfortune, such as the injury caused by Rāvaṇa and others.
The act of battle; *rabhasa* means "impetuosity" or "the force of joy," according to Amara (20).
Through separation comes sorrow, through seeing again comes joy, and through abduction—
Vrīḍā means shame;
by those [qualities], one is "jaḍaḥ," that is, devoid of comprehension. //2//

Regarding the term *cūlikā*: it is so called because events beginning with Sītā’s purification and ending with her departure are indicated by those remaining behind the curtain (*antarnaipathya*)—namely, the Magadha heralds, bards, and others.
As it has been said: "It is performed by those standing behind the curtain, such as the Magadha heralds, bards, and so forth."
"The introduction of the matter; this is the *cūlikā*, which is of many kinds.
(21) "Introduction" (*upakṣepa*) means indication (*sūcana*). //3//
"What doing," and so forth. "Kiṃkurvāṇaḥ" means a servant (*kiṅkara*);

by him they were "served," that is, watered at the proper time—for a servant indeed serves. "For the sake of joy" (*mude*); the word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied. Regarding "prarohasthalī":
the meaning is that from the time Laṅkā was seized by Kubera through victory, [Rāvaṇa's] valor remained unimpeded ever since.
He will say: "Both Laṅkā and this Puṣpaka aerial chariot were seized from the noble lord of the Yakṣas by the Ten-necked One. Thus, by each one [of these].
The construction is "by hundreds, by hundreds, in succession.
This refers to the seed (bīja) consisting of Rāmabhadra’s enthusiasm.
The disclosure [of the plot] through the mention of Rāvaṇa’s slaying is the structural element (aṅga) named *sandhi* (junction);
as it has been said: "The arrival of the seed [plot] is *sandhi*" (23). //4//

"Eastern" (*pūrveṇa*) and "western" (*paścimena*) end in the suffix *ena*; because of their connection with that [suffix], the rule "the second case is used after a word ending in *ena*" (*enapā dvitīyā*) applies.
"tvadarthīya," etc.: you yourself.

*Arthaḥ* means purpose (*prayojanam*). *Tvadarthaḥ*; by the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca* (Pāṇini 7.2.98), the substitution of *tvad-* occurs. In the sense of "desiring that for oneself," [the suffix *kyac* is added] after a *sup*-ending word by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ...* (Pāṇini 3.1.8).
Kyac; (27) therefore, the suffix *śatṛ* [is used].
The meaning is: "You alone are the purpose for both the Rākṣasa and the monkey host.
*Vyatikaraiḥ* means by collisions or crushings. *Karālāḥ* means deformed or hideous. (29)
"Sāhasrāḥ" means those possessing the number one thousand; the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of possession according to Pāṇini 5.2.127 (*aṇ ca*). "Patayaḥ" means lords.
Those who die in battle attain divinity;
this earth brings about the union of husband and wife—thus it intends their mutual coming together. (5)
"Having raised," and so forth.
There was only the sight of the jewel because the rest of the serpent and the tree were concealed by darkness. "Having raised it as a weapon. A *jyotiriṅgaṇa* is a firefly; [the term] *khadyota*...
"Jyotiriṅgaṇaḥ" (a firefly), according to Amarasimha; this is a designation containing a simile.
"Māyātamaḥ" refers to the darkness created by the *tāmisra* weapon. //6//
Chāyā: Noble son, have you also been brought here for the sake of Sītā, bound by the serpent-noose?
"For the sake of Sītā" means for the purpose of Sītā. "Brought" (sāhitāḥ);
From the verbal root *ṣaha* meaning "to endure," the suffix *ṇic* is applied; thus, the meaning is "made to experience" (*anubhāvitā*).
*Ām* is used in the sense of assent; Vardhamāna states: "Even *ām* is used in the sense of acceptance (*abhyupagama*)."

Regarding "carvita" and so forth: *khaṇiti* is an imitation of the sound of spitting upon a jewel (*maṇi*), according to the rule: "In the case of an indistinct imitation, [the suffix *ka* is added] when *it* follows *at*" (Pāṇini 5.4.57).

In the word *khaṇadit*, there is the substitution of the single form (*pararūpa*) for the vowel *a* [of the suffix *at*]; furthermore, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *iko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77), the augment *ṅamuṭ* is optional. //7//
"Aho" and so forth.
Herein lies the incongruity: that for a single object there are two sense organs, while for two objects there is a single sense organ as the perceiver;
that one travels with a chest [chest] unfit for traveling, and that one does not perform that [traveling] with feet intended for that purpose.
And there is the inhalation of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*).

He states this very point in the passage beginning with "two indeed," etc.; "in the instrument" (*karaṇe*) refers to the sense organ (*indriya*), with the intention of referring to its physical seat (*golaka*).
The dual number is used because they have two tongues; "one" is used because they have ears on their heads.
"Svadante" means they become sweet. "Mātā" is used in derision. The construction is: "If she gives birth again, she gives birth to exactly such [beings] as these."
A change in tone (kāku) is to be understood here; for this very reason, there is the expression "they laugh. //8//
In her affectionate smile, which was rooted in her recollection of Lakṣmaṇa’s valor—
Chāyā: My noble husband, what settlement, then, was the birthplace of that creeper of the fame of Saumitri?
"Kīrtiḥ, jitendrajit" means "fame, having conquered Indrajit"; the sense is, "where is the slaying of Indrajit? "Sākṣī" means a witness or observer.
"Pāda" means a peripheral mountain range.
(38) "A single witness" means that it is impossible even for sentient beings to perceive it. Alternatively, the word "pāda" [is used here].

It is a word denoting worship; for this very reason, there is the expression "the sole witness" (*ekasākṣī*). Indeed, the sole witness is worthy of worship. (39) Shadow—wherever this [shadow] appears: a certain night-stalker [is present], indicated by passion, horripilation, bristling hair, and perspiration.
Having fanned the funeral fire and then extinguished it, she follows her beloved in death.
Passion is directed toward the beloved; by means of the horripilation and perspiration born from it, the fire is successively inflamed and extinguished. //9//
"Bringing back," and so forth.
*Droṇaśaila* is the mountain containing the *sañjīvana* (life-restoring) herb. *Śalya* means suffering.
Regarding "free from thorns": the meaning is that had Indrajit not been slain by Lakṣmaṇa, even Rāvaṇa could not have been conquered by me. //10//
Smṛti (remembrance), directed toward Hanumān.
Chāyā: Noble son, where is he now—he who was the sole bearer of the burden of the camp of the Lord of Kiṣkindhā, and the kinsman to those distressed by the house of Raghu?
Hanumān is the sole bearer of the burden; the sense is that he has leaped across the ocean.
"Friend in adversity" means a kinsman in times of calamity. By this—

He connects [the passage] with the delivery of news concerning Rāmabhadra, beginning with the words "kṣuṇṇa" (crushed), etc. "By himself" means directly. "By his command" refers to the acceptance [of the task] out of affection.

He avoids [the literal sense]. By the word "procedure" (vidhi), the requisites (sambhāra) are indicated. This is the limb named "cessation" (nirodha), because it consists of the contemplation of what must be done immediately following the form of the consecration (abhiṣeka). As it has been said: "Cessation is the investigation of the task. (40)
Thus [ends section] 11.
"Lakṣmī" and so forth: [she is called] *yādas* because she was born from a *yādas*, which means an aquatic creature; the word "and" (*ca*) serves to include the state of being an aquatic creature.
The two words "api" (even) indicate the contradiction consisting in a single entity existing simultaneously in multiple locations. //12//
"Syādeva" and so forth:

if the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) were indeed the cause of the immortal, it would be entirely appropriate; that is, it would be logical. "Ekāntataḥ" means with absolute necessity. It would not be a marvel.
The meaning is that qualities of the cause, such as fluidity and sweetness, are observed even in nectar (amṛta). Vivarta,
on the other hand, is the appearance of another form without abandoning one's own essential nature.
Just as silverness [is superimposed] upon mother-of-pearl; but here, however,
there is merely a modification.
That which is perceived as a "vivarta" (illusory manifestation) is a marvel; the sense is that it is so because of the perception of a difference in kind (*vijātīyatva*). //13//
"Up to the throat," and so forth.
There is no visibility below the throat because it is covered by petals. The word "api" (also) [indicates] by means of the crest, the face, and so on.

He speaks of the impossibility of discerning the divisions of the back, belly, and so forth; however, that [discernment] is absent because his faces are situated in the four directions. Regarding the term *aravindanābha*, the suffix *ac* is applied here by the rule *ac-pratyanvava-pūrvāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.75).
By means of the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), the suffix *ac* is applied after the word *nābhi*. (43) 14.
"Vandata" means: because it is the place of origin for Lakṣmī and others, and the abode of Nārāyaṇa, it is worthy of worship; thus, there is an offering of salutation.
"Utsarpiṇī" means having an unimpeded flow; the syntactical connection is that whatever [is described] in this way is the Truth (Satya).
He says that very thing in the verse beginning with *jarayatu*: "May he cause to decay" (*jarayatu*) means "may he destroy. "May he fulfill" (*piparttu*) means "may he complete.
"May he bestow" (*dadhātu*) means "may he nourish. "As much as there is" (*yāvān tāvān*) refers to that which is immeasurable (*ameya*);
it is easily drunk (*īṣatpāna*). [The suffix] *yuc* is applied after a root ending in *ā* in the sense of the agentive suffix *khal*. (Pāṇini 3.3.129).
All this, in short, is the greatness of the dharma that takes the form of austerity. //15//
"Of the Sage," and so forth.
"Profundity" means unfathomability and invincibility. "Somehow" means it is impossible to describe.
The word "api" (even/somehow) [indicates this].

Regarding the estimation of the ocean: although it is exceedingly deep, [the poet says] "it fits within my palm," and thus its depth is described as even greater than that. Its loftiness (*uttuṅgatā*) consists of both its greatness (*mahimā*) and its height (*aunnatya*).
"Not high" expresses both stiffness and bowing;
"hahaha" [expresses laughter].
"Even for one born from a jar, such depth and loftiness—this is a marvel, meaning it is due to the greatness of his asceticism. //16//
"Jagat," and so forth.
"Jagadvigamaghasre" means on the day of the world's dissolution, i.e., the day of pralaya; according to Amara, "ghasra" means "day" (*dināhanī*).
"Ghasmarāḥ" means devourers; [the suffix] *kmarac* is applied after the roots *sṛ*, *ghas*, and *ad*. Of them...

"Of a thousand luminaries" means of a thousand suns known as the *saṃvartaka* fires; "massed together" because they have been fused by their radiance; "a peak" means a heap. "For a moment" means because of its destruction in the next instant. "Kālarudra" is the one named Saṅkarṣaṇa.
In that fire— the fire arising from his mouth— the sound *caṭaccaṭat* is an imitation of the sound of salt cracking; [this refers to] the word *caṭat*.

This is the form in the case where, following the rule *sarvasya dve* (Pāṇini 8.1.12), there is reduplication, and then, according to the rule *nāmreḍitasyāntyasya tu vā* (Pāṇini 8.1.2), the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) does not occur. *Sphuṭat* means "breaking apart" or "becoming pulverized," because salt breaks apart when it comes into contact with fire.
"Yāvatkṣaṇāt-kṣaṇādeva" means "from moment to moment. It is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule "yāvad-avadhāraṇe" (Pāṇini 2.1.8).
By the rule "nāvyayībhāvāt" (Pāṇini 2.4.83) and others, there is no elision (*sublopa*) of the case-ending, and the substitution of *ambhāva* occurs.

It does not exist; it did not exist (*nābhavat*), meaning by the force of the wind known as *saṃvartaka*; the present tense (*laṭ*) is used for the past according to the rule *laṭ sme* (Pāṇini 3.2.118). On this point, the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* states: "The *saṃvartaka* [wind] [drinks up] the moisture of the oceans, the body, and the earth..."

The sun drinks everything with its terrible rays and does not release anything at all. Then the fire of universal destruction (saṃvartaka), arising from the mouth of Saṅkarṣaṇa, burns the empty mountains with the force of the wind.
The cosmic egg shines as it is being consumed by the flames of fire and the sun from above, below, and all around,
like a ball of burnt cow-dung; then, a fierce wind [arises].
For more than a hundred years, the Khara wind blows as a destroyer, and the sky is shrouded in smoke and dust. (53) Thus [ends the seventeenth verse].
Chāyā: Noble son, what is this that is seen, appearing like a binding chain for the restraint of Jambūdvīpa, belonging to a ship situated in the midst of the ocean?
*Pota* means a vessel; as Amara states: "A vessel, however, is called *pota*. (54)

Together with Jambūdvīpa, for the purpose of restraint—that is, binding—like a fetter-bond; for a boat is indeed tied to the shore on trees and such by means of ropes and the like. [This describes] the nature of the bridge as being celebrated by Sugrīva.
Because it is bound to that [the sun] and makes that [the sun] manifest.
Shadow—By good fortune, the bridge appears like a great medicinal herb for the regrowth of the tree of hope for seeing my noble husband, which had been cut down. Blessed One, salutations to you!
"Yathā" and so forth.

"From afar," *āpātyāḥ* means "fallen upon"; this is established by the rule beginning with "bhavyageya" (Pāṇini 3.4.68). Regarding "easily accessible": for if one sees from a distance, the vastness [of the object] is not perceived.
And there is a similarity to a necklace (*hāra*) by virtue of its roundness. "Grāvan" means "stones" (*adrayaḥ*);
according to Amarasimha, "adri, gotra, giri, and grāvan" are synonyms for mountain. A "great hero" (*mahānāyaka*) is a central bead (*gulikā*) set with various jewels.
The specific central gem of a necklace. (57)//18//
"Mountains," and so forth.
"Mountains" refers to those hurled by the monkey. Here, the power of the waters arises from the impact of the mountains; therefore—
Thus is the expression "kallola"; according to Amarasimha, "the words *ullola* and *kallola* are used for great waves.
"Abhitāḍitānām" means those struck from the front; for this very reason, there is a cessation [of movement]. They are immovable (*acalāḥ*).
They are the very locus of its own arising; "source" (prabhava) means that it has issued forth from them—this is the intended sense. //19//
"Thus," and so forth.
They were pervaded by faith in the construction of such a bridge.
"By means of establishment" (*pratiṣṭhayā*) means by way of excellence; "increasing" (*vardhiṣṇuḥ*) means having grown great.

The suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied by the rule *alaṅkṛñ* etc.; according to Amara, *pratiṣṭhā* means "the greatness of stability. For this very reason, there is a movement in the opposite direction [of the mountains].
Of the *kṣoṇīdharas* (mountains), which constitute their own place of origin...
*Kuharāṇi* means cavities or pits. *Ahaṅkāraḥ* means surging [ego]. The phrase "the flood of water produced by the hurling of rocks" implies that it has subsided through the filling of those pits.
*Yadavasthaḥ* means in whatever state. "Do you remember"; [that] state.
The remainder [is as before]. //20//
"Setu," and so forth:
when it has "risen up" (uccalita), meaning it has moved upward;
and when it is "vain" (tuccha), meaning it is empty.
The rivers, by the power of time, bestow sweetness upon the particular fish dwelling within them, because those fish constantly experience a salty taste; "paṭutaram" means quickly.
They fell; for water falls swiftly from a height. //21//

"Immediately," and so forth. "Caverns" (*daryaḥ*) means mountain caves. By the word "having drunk," the great size of the caverns is indicated. "Twofold": the doubling [of tears] is due to the tears born from seeing their kinsmen. For indeed, in the camp, [tears flow] for the purpose of seeing the enemy.

Alternatively, because fires are kindled at night for the purpose of cooking, there is a similarity [to the present case], and thus it serves as a reminder (*smāraka*). By the term "at that time" (*tadātve*), the period of constructing the bridge is intended;
Amara states: "The word *tadātva* refers to that very time. //22//
Chāyā: Noble son, I know that Maināka, the crown prince of Gaurī’s father, the lord of mountains, who dwells in the midst of the ocean, has become immobile even without the severing of his wings.
The state of being a crown prince [is due] to his father's status as the king of mountains;
his immobility is due to the absence of flight.
"Laughing"—that is, disregarding both affection for his son and devotion to his father—[he said], "It is unjust..."
The abandonment of kin has indeed been performed; even though both wings were protected, they have become useless—this is the mockery.
He expresses this very point with the words beginning "the curlew" (*krauñcam*). What was done? It was done poorly.
...up to this point in the Harivaṃśa: "The glorious great mountain named Krauñca is the son of Maināka. (62) //23//
Chāyā: O King of Vimānas, my mind is blossoming with curiosity to wander upon the path of the sky; therefore, please ascend for a moment.
"Yathā" and so forth:
"apasarpanti" means they depart;
"yathā" and "tathā" are the two words [in question].
They are concerned with gradation; that is to say, a gradation in the division of directions is observed according to the gradation in ascending the Puṣpaka chariot. //24//
"Near," and so forth.
*Āśyānāḥ* means dried. *Pīḍitāḥ* means rubbed.
*Timyanti* means they become moist; [from the roots] *tima* and *ṣṭima*.
The verbal root is *ārdrībhāve* (in the sense of becoming moist). *Stanayitnavaḥ* means clouds.
For when rubbed with stones, the bark indeed becomes sapless. //25//

"Amī" and so forth. *Anāyuṣyam* means detrimental to life (*anāyurhitam*). *Āyuḥ* is the capacity for perceiving forms (*rūpagrahaṇa-śakti*). [The compound is formed] by the rule "khalayavamāṣa... and so forth, due to the inclusion of the particle *ca*.

The suffix *yat* [is applied] as in the word *avatamasam*. [This is derived from] *avasamandhebhyaḥ tamasaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.79), by which the suffix *ac* is applied. *Param* means "exceedingly. [It is] pervaded.
By "parimalaiḥ" is meant "by rays. (67) "Unobstructedness" is due to not being screened by clouds.
"Variegated" means possessing various colors. //26//
"Concealed," and so forth.
"Pravibhakti" means "division" (pravibhāga). "Pariveṣa" means for the purpose of protection, [as from] spirits and the like, because of distance.

There is a concealment of unevenness, and through the non-perception of specific features of the object, there is the perception of mere color. *Kuṭṭima* is an artificial ground; for it is protected from the trampling of cattle and other animals. (68)//27//
He replies regarding the earth and the ocean, which appear exceedingly small due to their extreme elevation: "This," and so forth.
"The very earth is the circle of hoods"; Amara states that "maṇḍala" has three genders. "One such as you."

The meaning is that you alone are the standard of comparison. "Something" (kim api) means beyond the reach of speech. You possess the quality of being a jewel (*ratnatva*) because you are the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*);

for Amara states: "A *ratna* [is used] also for the best of its own kind. Because of this quality of being a jewel, there is the expression of the word "priceless" (*anargha*); for Amara states: "*Argha* [is used] in the sense of value and in the ritual of worship."
Due to the presence of priceless jewels, there is pride; the sense is that even throughout the three worlds, it is the earth alone that is preeminent because of your proximity. //28//

Chāyā: Who is this mountain seen before us, as sweet as thousands of peaks of pure crystal resembling clusters of foam from the ocean being boiled by the mass of flames of the fire at the end of an aeon?
For when water is being boiled, the rising of froth occurs.
"Pura" and so forth: [it was for] Makaraketu; that is to say, for the sake of reviving Kāma. The dative case is used here in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*). (72)
For from the mountains medicinal herbs are born; thus the sense is that even Hara, whose passion had been withdrawn, became truly enamored of Pārvatī. //29//
Chāyā: Has the venerable Manmatha here also become an oblation in the fire of the eye on Śiva’s forehead?
The particle *api* is used here in the sense of a question.
*Durantaḥ* means death. Regarding the phrase beginning with *pura*: that which is called the *śṛṅgāṭaka* is connected to the palate and common to the pathways of the eyes.

The mouth is the opening of the channels of the eyes; regarding this, Vāhaṭa states: "At the junction of the four—the tongue, eyes, nose, and ears—there are four openings of the channels in the palate;
one who is pierced in these vital points (marmans), known as the *śṛṅgāṭaka*," [is lost].

"He immediately gives up his life" (73). Thus, his state of equal anger [extends] to the disturbances of the elements caused by anger that have arisen within himself, as well as to passion and so forth, with respect to those things connected to each of his own [senses].
Because it bestows [the fruit] without partiality through the paths of the three eyes,
"dhagaddhag" is an onomatopoeic imitation of the sound of blazing.
Because that [word] is not repeated, it lacks the nature of being an *amreḍita* (reduplication);

thus, it does not fall within the scope of the rule "but for the final [sound] of an *amreḍita*, optionally" (Pāṇini 8.2.34). However, when there is an imitation of a whole aggregate (*samudāyānukāra*),...
"Then indeed there is the form of another," so says the Kāśikā. (75) Some, not having considered this,
[claim] that this is merely an imitation of the word *prajvalana* itself, namely *dhagad*.
Having understood this, under the governing rule "sarvasya dve" (Pāṇini 8.1.1),
there is reduplication by the rule "nityavīpsayoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.1.4); and because of its status as an *āmreḍita* by the rule "tasya paramāmreḍitam" (Pāṇini 8.1.2).

By the rule "nāmreḍitasyāntyasya tu vā" (Pāṇini 6.1.99), which prohibits the substitution of the single substitute for the final vowel and consonant of the word *ad* when it is not an *amreḍita*, the substitution of the single substitute applies only to the final *t*.
Having applied [the rule], thinking that by the rule "ād guṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.87), a single *guṇa* vowel should result as "dhagaddhageti," they [proceed].
They say that "dhagaddhag" is a false reading; however, that is not correct, because in cases such as the blazing of fire,
there is experiential corroboration for the imitation of the collective sound itself, and because of the excellence of its composition.

The two words "api" (even/also) express the contradiction indicated by the disparity characterized by the arising and non-arising of the effect of anger, even though the status of being eyes is the same.

The resolution of that [objection] must be made on the basis of the difference in purpose: because the third [mantra] has the destruction of the world as its purpose, while the other two have protection as their purpose. //30//
"Blue," and so forth. "Antaḥ" means destruction itself;

it is the cause (hetu), and [the word is used] for its sake. This is because of the rule: "In the case of the words nimitta, kāraṇa, and hetu, all [case endings] are generally observed. Thus, the word *hetu* is employed here.

The fourth [analogy]: *sañjvalana* means that which causes blazing, such as fuel and the like. For just as a fire, once ignited, burns everything down to its very roots, so too does the world [burn] through the incineration of desire (*kāma*), which is the root of the world's arising.
The sense is that he has burnt it down to its very roots. //31//
Chāyā: Noble son, how is it that Mahādeva, being so merciless, has nonetheless returned to the Goddess?
"Tathā niranukrośaḥ" means "so merciless."

"Merciless," because his passion has been consumed; "compassion, pity, sympathy, and tenderness" are synonyms for *kṛpā*, according to Amarasimha (82). "To the Goddess"; the meaning is "in order to marry the Goddess."
The dative case is used according to the rule "kriyārthopapadasya" (Pāṇini 2.3.14). He has turned back;
the word "out of anger" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The sense is: having burnt away desire, how could he have come under the sway of desire?

"Smara," and so forth: since beauty and other such qualities are ineffective for the subjugation of this one who has conquered Smara (Kāma), he is without assistance. "With long [arrows]" means with those whose results are delayed; for one who is without assistance...

One does not obtain the fruit quickly; or rather, because there is an absence of other aids such as clever female messengers during the experience of passion and the divine union, [the efforts] are "long-lasting," meaning they persist until the emergence of the fruit.

The sense is that even when human effort and assistance are absent, the task can still be accomplished through destiny (*daiva*). Alternatively: because of his mastery over the senses and his freedom from attachment to friends and the like, [his efforts were] "long," meaning unimpeded; for from attachment...

Austerity is destroyed. They are called *subhagaṃkarana* because by means of them an unfortunate person (*asubhaga*) is made fortunate (*subhaga*). The suffix *khyun* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *āḍhya* (Pāṇini 3.2.56). That is the action; it is uncreated—that by which he [becomes so].
The Lord, by his own self— that is, by his own body—
conquers even in his own body as a second [being]; that is, a second body within a single body.
The word "api" (also) is used because of contradiction; the resolution is that it consists of two parts within a single body. The sense is that he became Ardhanārīśvara;
by this, an excess of love is indicated. //32//
"Long," and so forth.
*Tapasitvā* means "having practiced austerity"; [this is formed] by [the rule] *karmaṇo romanthatapobhyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.15).
By means of [the rule] beginning with "ityādinā," the form ending in *ktvā* is derived through the suffix *kyaṅ*. (86)
The sense is that since skulls and such are not fit to be given away, and there is no other wealth [to give], the body itself must be the object of donation. //33//
The practice of austerity toward one who possesses nothing is a laughable act born of folly.
Shadow: But in what kind of dwelling did the auspicious marriage ceremony of the Blessed One Sarvamaṅgalā take place?

Regarding the phrase "by the donor," and so forth: here, "great medicinal herbs" (mahauṣadhyaḥ) are intended to mean those that serve as antidotes to poisons such as snake venom; their status as antidotes applies even to mobile (jaṅgama) poisons.

This is because the stationary poison possesses fierce potency; as it is stated in the *Nidānapradīpikā*: "One should know that which is produced from bulbs, roots, and so forth as stationary poison (*sthāvara-viṣa*) of fierce potency; that which comes from snakes and the like is called mobile (*jaṅgama*)."
"It was fashioned from many substances. (87) For this very reason, Gaurī is fearless because the bracelet-like remainder is hidden.
*Kiśora* means a child. //34//
"O fathers," and so forth.

"Free from intoxication" (*nirmadāḥ*) means those whose intoxication has diminished. And this is because, in the winter, the youthfulness of snakes is lost; as it was stated by Vāhaṭa: "The poison..."

"The Darvīkara and other [serpents] respectively provoke Vāta and the other [humors], during youth, middle age, and old age, and in rain, cold, and heat. (88) For this very reason, the hand possesses a terrifying nature. //35//

Chāyā: Noble son, has Gaurī— rendered selfless by this very calamity that burns the body of Madana, and yet still distrustful— been united once more with the moon-crested Lord in her own physical form?
*Vyatikaraḥ* means a crowd or commotion. *Ātmamānaḥ* means pride;
its disappearance occurs because one's own desire, which causes self-exaltation, has been consumed by the fire of [Śiva’s] glance. This is due to her good fortune (*saubhāgyena*).
The poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) is that, because he cannot be brought under control, he is bound by force.
Regarding the passage beginning with "In this," etc.:
in such a situation, toward the woman who occupies his left side, there is laughter prompted by curiosity.
The exchange consists of the placement of a woman on the right side. //36//
"Regarding 'sambhoga' and so forth:

that which possesses a *vibhava*—meaning an abundance—that is being exceeded (*atiricyamāna*) or differentiated (*bhidyamāna*), is other than this; even the intense separation (*vipralambha*) of this couple is [in fact] enjoyment (*sambhoga*)."
The sense is that their mutual union remains in that very same state.
Alternatively, "vibhava" means "fruit"; in the world, the fruit of separation (vipralambha) is suffering, but for this [love], it is always [the opposite].
The meaning is that because joy arises from union, there is no difference in the fruit between the states of union (*saṃbhoga*) and separation (*vipralambha*).
Alternatively—*anatiricyamānaḥ* means "not exceeding" or "not additional. In the world, in *sambhoga* (union), only a single [state] is made the object of experience;
however, in *vipralambha* (separation), that very same [state] appears in manifold forms due to the conformity of mental states (*vṛtti-sārūpya*) arising from incessant remembrance.
Thus, *vipralambha* possesses even greater intensity than *sambhoga*. But here, even in *vipralambha*...

Because she is always present, there is an absence of recollection [of her as absent], and thus she is perceived as one alone; therefore, she is not distinct from the state of enjoyment (*sambhoga*). However, the possibility of separation (*vipralambha*) arises from a difference in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); as he will say: "Of whom [the Lord] is half..."

"The third eye, with its light spreading through the calamity of burning the universe, and with tears rising from compassion, produced a *simasima* sound as it struck against the other two eyes with mutual force. (89) Thus [it is said]. This—
In all three positions, the reason is "interwoven with one another. Regarding that which is in the couple: it is that the other lord [Śiva] must stand on the left limb—the right side—of the Goddess.
Curiosity is longing;
at the time of looking into the mirror, she allays— that is, restrains—
it by saying, "You are standing on the right side alone."
For the reflection is seen as reversed; or rather, that which is in the right part of the mirror [is perceived as] "I"— that is curiosity, meaning joy— and that [joy].

He refutes [the objection] by saying, "This state is not ultimately real, because it is established as being merely a false reflection"; however, there is a sense of wonder because the right side of the body is worthy of worship; [and thus he says], "The left..."
"Of the right and left," according to the *Viśvaprakāśa*.
(37) (90) "Svacchanda," etc.
One's own *chandaḥ* is one's intention; according to Amarasimha, "intention, *chandaḥ*, and disposition (*āśaya*) are synonyms. For the breast is indeed a cause of ridicule for a man.
*Matam* means consent or approval. *Prācīnāvītam* refers to [the sacred thread] over the right shoulder.
Its retention [is required],
and that is because it is unsuitable for a woman; he who has a third eye, sequentially on the right and left sides.
From the friction of the force of tears in the form of flames arising from wrath and compassion,
making a specific sound imitating the syllable *simasima*; on the right is the flame of Rudra.
Because it has the purpose of destroying the world; and because, on the left,
through the mere presence of the consciousness of the Goddess who is the primordial nature (prakṛti), she brings about the production of the universe.
Out of grief, as if at the loss of her own child. //38//
Regarding "sveda" and so forth: perspiration arises from union with a beloved.
By metaphorical extension (*upacāra*), the drying of the perspiration resting upon the decorative leaf-designs (*patrabhaṅga*) is itself called the "drying of the leaf-designs."

Because it is unfit to be designated as "woman" and so forth due to its association with both feminine and masculine genders, it is called "the fourth"; for it is said: "It is neither woman nor man, thus it is neuter," and "It is not a brother" (92).
"In such sūtras as these, the neuter gender of the words 'strī' and 'pums' occurs precisely because they are treated as irregularly formed (nipātita) terms," so says Vardhamāna. (93)//39//
"He assumes," and so forth;
because the arms of Hari served as the support for Mount Mandara.

The meaning is: because the limbs have become wrinkled from the friction of the tips of the diamonds set in those armlets, we infer that even now—after the period of churning—this [mountain], though its base has been worn away by rubbing against the shell of the tortoise, is still as high as it was before, or perhaps even higher. //40//

"Tattādṛg" and so forth: the rubbing of the rope in the form of Vāsuki of such a kind; "samyagrūḍhāyāḥ" means of that which has healed, i.e., become calm; "pakṣacchidāyāḥ" refers, by metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), to a wound.
By the striking, even that which is *aruntuda*—causing agony;

[the suffix] *khaś* is applied here according to the rule *vidhvaruṣostudaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.35). The word *aho* is used because the rubbing of a wound is unbearable. By the evil-minded one—that is, by one with a corrupted inner self. Of Lakṣmī...
Perversity (*vāmatā*) arises from producing the inequality of wealth and poverty in the world;
it is "diverse" (*vyasta*), meaning characterized by distinctness. //41//

"With agitation" (*sāvegam*): there is agitation because she, who belongs to the opposing side, defiles the fortune of her own faction. For this very reason, the moon, who belongs to that [opposing] faction, causes her distress.
He refutes [this] with the words "by this," and so forth.
The commentary [states]: "By this very [ocean], which has been reduced to a mere residue of cream after the ocean of milk was churned, having extracted the moon..."
A violent assault was launched against women whose husbands were away;
Maṇḍa has escaped.
Yavāgū (gruel);

as it has been said: "Maṇḍa is that which is devoid of grains. That of which only the residue remains—when the nectar, moon, and so forth have been extracted—is milk alone remaining; thus, it is essence-less.
Up to: *Ārabhaṭī* is the mode (*vṛtti*) that manifests the terrible sentiment (*raudra-rasa*).

As it has been said: "The *Kaiśikī* [mode] is in the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), the *Sāttvatī* in the heroic (*vīra*), and the *Ārabhaṭī* in the terrible (*raudra*), the odious (*bībhatsa*), and everywhere."
"Bhāratī" (96)—by this, anger is indicated; the meaning is that he is angry with women separated from their lovers.
"To cast," etc.: *valate* means he exerts himself. We desire to cast Lakṣmī into the ocean, yet, like the moon, once again...
The meaning is: "We do not cast [it] out for fear that it will come together [with others]. //42//
"Regarding 'to someone' and so forth:
because Viṣṇu is the originator of all deceptive traditions,
[the text speaks of this] in order to grasp the deception issuing from his own mouth."

The sense is that his residence is upon the boundary of her chest; for this very reason, he is called Kaiṭabharipu (the Enemy of Kaiṭabha), as it is well known in the Devīmāhātmya that he conquered Kaiṭabha through Māyā. He...
For it is well known that a *rākṣasa* is skilled in illusion. Salutation is for one who is free from anger; for attachment to anger leads to fault. We speak—that is, we ask.
*Vidyāgṛha* means a house for the practice of learning.

*Ācāryakam* means the work of a teacher; [the suffix] *vuñ* is applied according to the rule beginning with "from a word having *ya* as a penultimate letter" (*yopadhāt*, Pāṇini 5.1.132). The practice of learning, which consists in attaining what is lower and even lower than the low, [is performed] from the presence of water.
"What? Did his dwelling likewise become a lotus situated right there?"—this constitutes two questions. //43//
Slandering Lakṣmī by means of the ground of her subservience to Sītā, he says,
"O you who [dwell] among gods and asuras," and so forth. By the term *ārabhaṭī*, he refers to the dance characterized primarily by that [style].

It is observed: therein, for the musicians, *tāla* is a specific rhythmic division, and there the dancer [performs]; the meaning is that she moves about precisely where there is the sound of victory-trumpets. For kings, in their humiliation—that is, in bringing about improper conduct—[she acts].

*Kharjūrī* is a specific kind of liquor; the meaning is that it intoxicates like wine (*surā*). *Khadyotinī* (the "glittering one") is a term of reproach for *kharjūrī*. *Sahaḥ* means strength; they exist together with that.

Thus—[they are] rash men; [the suffix] *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule "after *ojas*, *sahas*, and *ambhas*, [the suffix *ṭhak* is added]" (Pāṇini 4.4.27). The sense is that he plays (*khelati*) where there is the falling of weapons. By the word *khadyotī*, he expresses insignificance.
"Like a flash of lightning" expresses instability.
"By those possessing qualities," and so forth: *guṇas* are virtues such as valor, as well as ropes.
"A high station" means greatness.
And the term *unnatapadam* (the elevated place) flashes forth [in the mind], for a rope is indeed the means for ascending to a high place.
*Asidhārāvratam* is a specific kind of austerity; for one who, in secret, [approaches] a beautiful and adorned woman...
Having placed a woman on one's lap,
it is like standing on the edge of a sword, in that the mind remains free from desire for her.
It is so named because of its difficulty; previously,
due to bad associations, one falls into a low state, and therefore, for the sake of turning away from that and achieving association with the virtuous, [one should practice] on the sword-blade.
By means of this poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), a jest is revealed. //44//
Commentary: People, rendered helpless by the perverse play of their own destiny, sing songs of ill-repute regarding Fortune.
"Destiny" (*daiva*) means luck; as it is said: "Destiny (*daiva*), fate (*diṣṭa*), fortune (*bhāgadheya*), and luck (*bhāgya*)."
Thus says Amara: "Duryaśas" means ill-repute, base conduct, and so forth;
the meaning is that they themselves, being unfortunate, revile Fortune as being fickle.
Chāyā: Who is this mountain, which resembles a mass of moonlight enveloped by the day?

*Kroḍīkṛtaḥ* means gathered into a heap (*rāśīkṛtaḥ*). *Vicchardaḥ* means a collection (*samūhaḥ*). It is like the piling up at night of grain and the like that were spread out during the day, or the piling up during the day of moonlight that was spread out at night.
The sense is that this is logical.
Regarding the passage beginning with "so'yam" (this is that):
here, the word *sphaṭika* refers to any pure stone in general; [it is used] in the presence of a crystal.
Because it does not convey a reflected image.

"Shadow" (*chāyā*) is an object that is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of sunlight. "Even though hidden" (*pītāpi*) means even though concealed; the sense is that light radiates in all directions.

By "pratikṛtibhiḥ" is meant "reflections. Although [the sun] is yellow, it is made present [in the water]; thus, the apparent contradiction is to be resolved by understanding that the word *chāyā* refers to a reflection.
For *chāyā* means the beloved of the sun, or luster.
"Pratibimba means 'without sunlight,'" according to Amara.
*Mudrām* means contraction. *Uddāmānaḥ* means unrestrained.
The meaning is that, by virtue of its support, even a mere line of the moon may surpass the sun. //45//
"Hanta" and so forth.
"Without satiety" means that there is no satisfaction regarding the object of curiosity; and that—
The sense is that it manifests the strength of Rāvaṇa’s own conquest.
He states this very point in the verse beginning with "the mountain" (*giri*) and so forth. Here, the word *maṇi* refers to the diamond (*vajra*), as other gems [are not intended].

Because it is impossible for the stone to have been worn by friction; and because at the time of its uprooting, his arm was pressed against it, the surface of the stone was marked with the seal of a makara within the leaf-designs of the diamond-studded armlet.
"Even of the city of the Lord of Serpents" [is said] because crystal illuminates objects situated on its opposite side.
The resolution of the contradiction—consisting in the illumination of a remote object of meaning indicated by the word *api*—is [as follows]. //46//
"Ten-faced," and so forth.
"Pīḍitāḥ" means bent down;
for a region pressed by a staff indeed sinks. Precisely for this reason...

The bliss of Śiva, who resides in its center like one upon a sacrificial altar—Amara states that "vitardi" means a "vedikā" (altar)—is experienced there. The description of it as a "water-house" (*jalagṛha*) arises from the resemblance between the rays of the crystal and a downpour of water. //47//
"Kailāsa," and so forth.
"Kandalitābhiḥ" means sprouted.
"Nadīmātṛkāḥ" refers to those who subsist on river water and irrigation channels. (105)
*Hastaguṇa* means having hands that are like nectar; by that, there is the growth of trees—this is a worldly convention.
*Dhātreyakabhrātā* means one who is like a son of a nurse (*dhātrī*).
The brothers; the *dhātrī* is the foster-mother, and she is Gaurī, because she nurtures the tree by watering it.

Of the one who has ascended (*upoḍhasya*), that is, of Kumāra, the six-faced one (*ṣaṇmukhasya*), the childhood sports (*śiśukrīḍāḥ*) consist of tossing about, shaking, and so forth; the brothers are those who accompany these.

For they endure the pressure of their brothers; therefore, they nourish brotherly affection. That is to say, even amidst such pressure, they flourish precisely because their tenderness remains unimpaired.
In the reading "puṣpyanti," the reading "sahoḍhā" [is used].
"Sahoḍhāḥ" means "together"; "puṣpyanti" means "they become blossomed."
The root *puṣp* in the sense of "blooming" belongs to the *divādi* class. (48)

"Sahasra" and so forth. "Namasisitari" means "while one is performing salutation"; the form is derived from the root *nam* with the suffixes *kyac* (according to Pāṇini 3.1.19, *namovarivaḥ...*) and then *tṛc*.
When [the lover], characterized by his limbs, brings himself— [possessing] a resemblance between his eyes and blue lotuses—
to the vicinity of her feet, she becomes impetuous with joy during their play.
When [the snake] desires to seize [the child], thinking it to be a garland, laughter arises from the recognition of both delusion and fickleness. //49//

Regarding the passage beginning with "yannāṭye": in the dance called *tāṇḍava*, [the world] is situated upon a revolving terrestrial sphere (*bhramyā*); for this very reason, there is constant rotation. By the words "day" (*vāsara*) and "night" (*niśā*), light and darkness are indicated.

During Rudra’s cosmic dance of dissolution, when the earth revolves due to the force of its rotation and even Mount Meru revolves throughout the day and night, by that momentum— and not according to the measure of its own time— it [the mountain] completes a full circuit in a mere instant.

Lightning-flashes are said to appear repeatedly within the range of vision as both light and darkness; let them be considered luminous (taijasa) because they are perceived, yet they are also born of darkness (tāmasa).
The word *katham* expresses wonder;

it is a wonder because [such a thing] has never been seen before. *Antyeṣṭi* refers to the *paitṛmedhika* oblation; one who performs that is a *yajvā*, meaning, in effect, a destroyer of the world. //50//
"Victorious," and so forth.
The deer-marked [moon] experiences fear due to the delusion that it is a lion's claw.
Precisely because of this retreat, there is the state of being stainless; [this refers to] the digit (kalā).
Thus, its intrinsic stainlessness is figuratively conceived as a "mark" (*lakṣmī*).
Regarding the word "mind" (*manaḥ*), there is an absence of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. //51//
To cast a stain upon that [the moon] as well, he says: "etassa" and so forth. The commentary:
of this Lord of Spirits (bhūtanātha) who dwells in the cremation ground and is adorned with a garland of skulls from the human crania of the Dandaśūka hell.
The stain upon the beloved of Rohiṇī (the Moon) is merely a mockery of an ornament. Of what use is that wretched deer?
"Dandaśūkāḥ" means serpents; "karoṭiḥ" means a skull-bone.
A garland of shaven heads (*muṇḍamālā*) is a garland made of severed heads; *viḍambana* means imitation;
[the phrase] "of Rohiṇī’s beloved" refers to the Moon.

This is a statement of good fortune (*saubhāgyokti*). The intention is that, because of its similarity to it, there is a censure of the ornament by treating it as an ornament for one who is not to be touched (*aspṛśya*). "Wretched" (*tapasvin*) means pitiable;
the sense is: "this is not the deer's fault. (112)
He humorously dismisses the idea that the moon’s ornamentation is a cause for censure with the words beginning "śaṅke" (I suspect), etc.
[The passage beginning with] "sahacara," etc., refers to the fact that at night, by their own will, Piśācas...
To that serenity which arises from wandering at will; for indeed, during the day, the *piśācas* have their movement obstructed by the sun.
As it is said in the *Prabodhacandrodaya*: "When the orb of the sun is risen, how [can they move]?"
"How can there be room for piśācas when the orb of the sun is blazing?"— thus [it is asked]. "The maker of night" (niśākara).
It contains the reason for the subject matter at hand. //52//
Rāma’s great respect [for Sītā] was for the sake of avoiding the censure directed at her, and because of his contemplation of her being an ornament of Śiva.
Therefore...
Thus he says: "Of Śrīkaṇṭha," and so forth.
*Kaparda* refers to the matted locks (*jaṭājūṭa*) of Hara. *Grāmaṇī* means a lord (*prabhu*); [as it is said: "The word *grāmaṇī* is used for a barber in the masculine... (Amara-kośa 3.5.28).
"Śreṣṭha" means "the head of a village" in three senses, according to Amara.

[The term] *daṃśaka* (stinger/bite) is used because of being oppressed by the binding of the book; for a serpent indeed bites when it is oppressed. *Kalikām* is a metaphor (*rūpaka*); [it refers to] a pair of tongs (*sandaṃśikā-yanttra*).
A *nābhyāyasa* is a specific kind of furnace that seizes [the metal] while it is being heated.
It is "turned" (or heated), meaning it is subjected to intense heat; the sense is that just as a lump of silver is heated for the purpose of fashioning vessels and the like, so too is this [metal].
There is a similarity between a digit of the moon and silver, and between a snake and a mechanical device. //53//
"Of Meru," and so forth. "The luminaries" refers to the sun and others.
The fact that the shadows move upward indicates the height of the mountain. Regarding the phrase "when they have been drunk up": [the sun] drinks the first [shadow].
"The fire [is] the second," and so forth;

the meaning described regarding the origin of the moon should be understood here. The "wildness" (ucchṛṅkhalatva) of the deer is due to the absence of the bolt in the form of the digits (kalā). //54//
"Of the land," and so forth.
By "fruits," it is meant that the "subsequent ones" are superior; for it is said, "a region containing gold within yields greater fruit."
The meaning is: "renowned for its golden treatises"; how much more so, then, for all gold? Regarding the word *sīmanta*: *sīmanta* means that which creates a twofold division, as by a path.
The earth is divided into two parts. The term "sīmanta" (parting line) is used because the feminine nature [of the earth] is perceived through it.
A "ghaṇṭāpatha" is a road suitable for the passage of elephants and other large animals.

"A *ghaṇṭāpatha* is a *saṃsaraṇa*" (118), according to Amara; "it is said that a *saṃsaraṇa* is a path for elephants and other animals that is free from congestion," according to Bhoja (119). *Pradhi* means the rim of a wheel; "the rim of a wheel is the *pradhi*, the *nemi*" (120), according to Ajaya. [The word] *kathañcana* [is used here].
Because one who is submerged in mud is difficult to extricate. //55//
"Etāsu" and so forth:
(121) *vāṭikā* means a row; *pakṣa* means a side. For this very reason, even at midday, there is lengthiness of the shadow. //56//

*Uparyupari* means "in the immediately adjacent upper region"; the reduplication is according to *Pāṇini 8.1.7*: *upary-adhy-adhasaḥ sāmīpye*; and [the doubling of the following word] is according to *Pāṇini 8.1.8*: *dhig-upary-ādiṣu triṣu*.
By such statements, the second [case] is expressed.
*Puṣkalāvarttakas* are a specific class of clouds.
(124) The word "how" (*katham*) expresses wonder that Airāvaṇa roams even here, since his confinement by Rāvaṇa has now ceased.
Because particles have multiple meanings,
[the phrase] "on this day," and so forth, is explained as follows: the distinction is that *srajaḥ* (garlands) are to be worn on the head, while *dāmāni* (strings) are to be worn around the neck.
Regarding the word *sragdāmnīm*: the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.28). Today, [these things] are difficult even for Indra to obtain.
The statement regarding the well-being of heaven implies that even the women of one's kinsmen have enjoyed [the fruits] there properly;
by the verse beginning with "yanmālya" (126), its unassailability even by Indra was previously stated; for this very reason, there is freedom from enmity.
The second half [of the verse] states his prior condition: *paricchadaḥ* means "attendant" or "companion";
*pratīcchan* means "receiving" or "maintaining"; the *kanduka-samādhi* (the ball-concentration) is to be inferred here;
*sāṃrāviṇam* means "pervasive."

The act of sounding (*śabdana*); [the suffix] *inuṇ* is applied in the sense of "pervasion" (*abhividhi*) according to Pāṇini 3.3.45 (*abhividhau bhāve inuṇ*); then [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied according to 5.4.15 (*aṇ-inuṇ-aḥ*);
and [the feminine suffix] *ī* is applied according to 4.1.76 (*inaṇ-ī-anapatye*).
Due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), there is no elision of the *ṭi* suffix by the rule *na-staddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.143). //57//
"In a non-range" means in a place that is not their range; "they move about" is the ellipsis.
Regarding the phrase "each one," etc., the word "one" (*eka*) here—

Because it denotes the primary [meaning] and lacks the expression of the number one, the plural form is used; by the rule "ekaṃ bahuvrīhivat" (Pāṇini 8.1.9), there is reduplication and the treatment as a *bahuvrīhi* compound; for this very reason...
There is elision of the middle *su*;
the meaning is that there are many excellent ones. They are either well-known or established in the intellect.

"Those who possess arms" means the strong; "they dwell"—the word "in the world" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "From whom?"—this constitutes the status of the recipient (*sampradāna*) according to the rule *krudhadruha* (Pāṇini 1.4.37). "We contend"—that is to say, with whom do we oppose ourselves by determining [their] relative superiority?
For in the world, one who determines relative superiority [acts] toward one who has been humiliated...
She becomes an enemy. "Wearing" (*ābibhratī*) means adorning herself;
she was born in a field of heroes—that is, on earth, Rāvaṇa alone was considered a hero.
"Challenging" (*āhvayamānam*) means challenging out of rivalry; according to the rule *spardhāyām āṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.31).
Thus [it is] the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). "Enam" means Rāvaṇa; "cakre" means he has insulted him.
That the middle voice is used for the sense of "insulting" (*avakṣepaṇa*) is according to the rule beginning with *gandhana* (Pāṇini 1.3.32).
We perceive that insult because his two eyes were made [to be struck]; thus, by the rule on verbal roots (*dhātu*), [the middle voice applies].
The remainder [is the Self]. We hear it, for the Creator fashioned our two ears; through the presence of both eyes and ears, there arises the capacity to see and the capacity to hear.
The sense is that they are unable to speak because their lifespan is limited. Regarding the word *alpa*:
by the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.27] beginning with "prathama-," it receives the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*).
Alternatively: *enam* refers to Rāvaṇa; *yat* refers to the action, namely the confinement within the armpit and so forth.

He made (cakre); here the root *kṛ* is transitive (*dvikarmaka*), because it is included in the list beginning with *ji* and *daṇḍi*. Since we perceive that [object], the eyes are the instrument; thus, "made" means "accomplished in its purpose."
"Since we hear [it], therefore [we have] ears; [it is] accomplished = its purpose is fulfilled"; for such an activity as has been described is neither seen nor heard of before. //58//

Thinking, "Rāvaṇa is such a person, yet Vālin acted in this way," and unable to endure the disparagement of Rāvaṇa, he says: "Is he to be spoken of? and so forth. "Vācyaḥ" means capable of being spoken; [this is derived] from the rule *śaki liṅ ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.172).
Is he to be censured because he is inferior to Rāvaṇa? Or rather, it is he who,
having surpassed Rāvaṇa,
has traversed the earth.
The excellence of Vālin is to be praised;
or is he to be censured as being inferior to [Rāma]? Regarding his "subduing"—that is, his killing—his "conduct of destruction" refers to the act of slaying Vālin.
To a slight degree— only in matters such as learning news of Sītā and building the bridge— was he helpful; Vālī was slain by me with ease and without any assistance,
whereas Rāvaṇa [was slain] with the aid of Sugrīva and others.
The sense is that he is superior even to Vālin, because [Vālin] was difficult to overcome even with efforts such as the construction of a bridge. //59//
Chāyā: Noble son, what indeed is this that is seen, white as a cluster of crushed camphor and agate, filling the courtyard of the sky?
*Karpūraśilā* is a specific mineral of white color. *Guccha* means a cluster or collection.

Beginning from the state prior to its rising, he describes the successive stages up to the state of the moon's emergence with the words "yaṃ prāk" (that which [was] before), and so forth. *Sambibhratam* means nourishing; for when the moon has risen...

The intended meaning is that the conventional usage of "east" and so forth arose from [the positions of] Mount Meru and the other mountains; that is, "the conventional usage of east and so forth arises from the conjunctions of the moon and other celestial bodies with Mount Meru."

Or rather, its status as the cause for conventional designations such as "east" and so forth is established by scriptural authority (śāstra). That which [destroys darkness] even before [the moon rises], by means of its streams of shimmering light— that is, its rays— is therefore the seed of the mountain of sunrise.
Because of the emergence of the moon-like sprout of form which is the support of light, one lives in order to see;
the meaning is that seeing itself is the fruit of living.

It is designated as "the fruit of living" because it is the means for attaining the abundance of worldly and otherworldly welfare (*śreyaḥ*), which constitutes the fruit of living, just as in the expression "clarified butter is life."

The fact that the first sight of the crescent moon is a means for attaining spiritual welfare is stated in the *Ṛgvidhāna*: "With the hymn beginning 'O Soma,' one should look at the moon as it rises; month after month, one should worship it with fuel in hand."
Month after month, he shall not experience those threefold sufferings;
he shall obtain garments and attain the same world as the Moon— thus [said] Gautama.
"Previously, the destruction of one's own death was seen.
(140) Regarding the phrase "like a sprout": just as one desires to see the first sprout with devotion, [so too does one desire to see the cessation of death].
In the same way, this [person] too; therefore, you must look upon him—this is the meaning. //60//
He states the origin [of the word] with "sa śrīkaṇṭha... and so forth. *Kuṭṭima* is an artificial ground;
this is because he wears matted hair (*jaṭā*). *Pariṣkāra* means ornament; for an artificial ground is indeed adorned by a lamp. *Kukṣimbhari* means one who fills his belly.
That is to say, "the destroyer of darkness.
According to the rule *phalegrahirātmambhariśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.26), the word *kukṣimbhari* is also correct due to the inclusion of the particle *ca*. A *saṃskartā* is one who adorns or embellishes.
By the rule "samparyupebhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.137), the suffix *suṭ* is applied. For a woman, when adorned, is pleasing to those who desire her. *Rasavatī* means a kitchen;
*paurogava* is its superintendent—that is to say, the provider of delicious food (*sudhāprada*). [In the context of] *rasavatyām*...
"But *pākasthāna* is the kitchen (*mahānasa*); *paurogava* is its superintendent," so says Amara (1.7.14). //61//

He states the manifestation: "prāṇāyāma," and so forth. By the word *prāṇāyāma*, which primarily denotes the restraint of the vital breath (*vāyu*), its resulting contraction is indicated; for this very reason, the term *muni* (sage) is used. Of the intoxication of youth, which stands in the place of the hero—
The *līlās* (amorous sports) occupy the position of the heroines; together with them, in social gatherings— that is, in conversations—
the *pīṭhamarda* acts as an assistant, one who awakens the transformations of youth.
As it is said in the *Rasakalikā*, in the section on assistants (*sahāya-prakaraṇa*): "The *pīṭhamarda*, the *viṭa*, as well as the *ceṭa* and the *vidūṣaka*. (145) *Āśaḥ* means food to be eaten.
From the root *aś* in the sense of "eating" (Pāṇini 1.46), the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the passive sense (Pāṇini 3.3.18–19); [this refers to] the eyes of women.
*Prātarāśaḥ*: meaning that which satisfies the eyes.

*Āyuṣṭomaḥ*: a specific *homa* (oblation) for longevity; the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs according to the rule "the *stoma* of *jyotis* and *āyus*" (Pāṇini 8.3.108); it is an inflamer of desire.
This is the meaning: *maunamudrā* is the state of being closed like a bud (*mukulanam*);
*anurāgaḥ* is love (*premā*). He by whom love has been stilled is "one who has brought love to rest";
thus, he is "one who has caused [the bud] to blossom."
Up to this point, it has been established that *śṛṅgāra* alone is the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and no other; that is to say, at the rising of the moon, *śṛṅgāra* eclipses all other flavors.
It "prevails" (*vibhavati*), meaning it becomes capable [of manifesting]. //62//

Regarding the manifest stain caused by the manifestation of the [moon's] orb, he says "karṇottaṃsa" and so forth. "Having done" means having placed [it]. By saying "having laughed together," he indicates that the gathering was rooted in jest.

*Saṃhūtaḥ* means summoned by many; Amara states: "The word *saṃhūtiḥ* refers to that which is performed by many. *Kṣubhitaḥ* means agitated, having moved due to the desire to devour sprouts of barley.

Because it is composed of fragments, it is a patched garment (*kanthā*). "Constantly" means month by month; it is loose due to repeated joining and falling apart. What should one do? Into what state should one bring it? The potential mood (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of deliberating upon what ought to be done (150). "Should one cause it to fall apart?"—this is the inquiry.

The word *yuvatī* is grammatically correct when the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule "some say [it is added] after any [stem] ending in a vowel other than *kṛt*," as stated in the *Nyāsa* commentary: "after any [stem] ending in a vowel, whether it is a *kṛt*-derived suffix or not. //63//

One should not form a joint that has been disarticulated; rather, one should act in this manner—as stated in the passage beginning with "romantha" and so forth. "Romantha" refers to the movement of the jaw by animals when their bodily elements (dhātus) are in a state of equilibrium; for this very reason...
The state of being seated at ease; and this is because of their perpetual satisfaction due to the proximity of the moon (*sudhāṃśu*).

"Siddhas" refers to a particular class of divine beings (*devayoni*). "With cymbals" means with the sounds of bronze cymbals (*kāṃsyatāla*); "he shall not break it" (*mā bhāṅkṣīt*) means he will not destroy it; [this is according to the rule] *māṅi luṅ*.
The *luṅ* suffix is used for future meaning; as stated in the *Kāśikā* (155), "it is an exception to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*s).
[This occurs] in the sense of "he will be" (*ghaṭanayā*) in the month.
Because it is new, it will not break due to its firmness; however, "kṣubhitaḥ" means moved by fear. The word "duḥkhāya" is used in the sense of purpose (tādarthye).
The fourth [case ending] will be used; it shall be in the future tense. //64//
In connection with this occurrence, he says "of this" and so forth. "Of the color" means of the white color; "line" means a streak.
Furthermore, since the reconstitution must be performed by the very same parts as those of the previous color, it is held [there] for the purpose of determining that color. //65//
Regarding the phrase "revered by existence" (*bhavādṛta*), he praises [the Lord] with two verses beginning with "Thou, O Gīrvāṇa... out of devotion (*bhaktyā*).
*Śrāddham* means that which is given with faith (*śraddhayā*); it is used here in the sense of being for the sake of that (*tādarthye*).
The fourth [case]: (157) the function of the nurse (*dhātrī*) is nourishing (*poṣaṇa*), because she satiates [the child] with nectar (*amṛta*).
The word *vīrudh* (creeper) is indicative of medicinal herbs and the like, since food arises from them.
*Giran* means swallowing.
*Tacchalena* means by means of the pretext of poison. Who could he be? No one at all by his voice.
The meaning is "it would be so. That is to say, even one who has consumed poison becomes healthy through wearing you. //66//
"Of the eyes," and so forth.
*Madhuparka* is a specific drink consisting of curd, honey, and ghee mixed together; here, however, it refers to moonlight (*jyotsnā*).
*Satra* means its constant offering—that is, giving it perpetually. [The word *satra* is used in the senses of "covering" and "sacrifice."]

According to Amara, *sadādāna* means "that which always gives," which is to say, that which satisfies the eyes. *Medaskara* means "nourisher," for nourishment indeed comes about through fat (*medas*).

*Rasāyana* is a strengthening medicine. *Gañjā* is the place of nectar-like wine; according to Amara, "gañjā is a tavern" (159), meaning, in effect, a provider of ambrosia (*sudhā*). It is the ocean known as Kṣīroda.
Its shell is that of the *dākṣāyaṇīs*, meaning the offspring of Dakṣa, i.e., the stars; for Amarasimha states:
"The *dākṣāyaṇīs* are the stars beginning with Aśvinī. [The word] *dakṣāyaṇī* means the offspring (*apatyam*) of Dakṣa; [the suffix *-āyaṇi-* is applied] by [Pāṇini 4.1.95]: *ata iñ*.

By the rule *iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95); and by the rule *kauravyamāṇḍūkābhyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.19), because the word *ca* has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned, there is the suffix *ṣpha*; and by the rule *ṣidgaurādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.41).
*ṅīṣ*. "What shall we praise? means that his greatness is impossible to praise.
This is the ornament named *guṇakīrtana* (praise of qualities), because it consists of the celebration of the moon's qualities through names such as *madhuparka* and *satra*;
as it has been said: "Of those possessing qualities..."
Where there is the mention of one [person] by means of names, that is the praise of qualities (guṇakīrtana). (165) //67//
In the context of the phrase "the leader of the daughters of Dakṣa," he says by way of this connection: "Āryaputra" (Noble Son).
The commentary (*chāyā*) states: "O Noble Son, [this honor] has been placed upon the heads of even those co-wives who are equal in family, beauty, and youth."
By that blessed daughter of the Dakṣa lineage, the venerable Moon was heard of as "the lover of Rohiṇī" and as "one who has given a foot (caraṇa)";
this implies she was superior even to them.
"Dear one," and so forth. The equality of enjoyment arises because [the deity] abides for sixty *ghaṭikās* within all the lunar mansions (*tārā*).
Among these, there is something indescribable: the good fortune born of her husband's affection, and the weight of her beauty and virtues.
= Fragrance //68//

Having observed his outstretched hands, he says "dalita" and so forth. "Ūṣmaiva" means treatment (*upacāra*); it is an empirical fact that when the doors and such of a house or similar structure are closed, heat (*ūṣman*) arises once the door-panels and other obstructions are removed. "Jāḍyam" refers to the state of the limbs being stiffened by cold. "Kṣaṇa... [and so on].

[The word *kṣaṇa* ends] in another [sense] with the suffix *uṣman*, due to the disappearance [of the final vowel]. *Abhisṛmarāḥ* means "female messengers" (*abhisārikāḥ*), according to Pāṇini 3.2.166:
*sṛghasyadaḥ kmarac*.

Their state of being mute (*mūkatva*) is due to their role as female messengers (*abhisārikā-dūtītvāt*); and that [muteness] is because they indicate the path and because they act as instigators (*prerakatvāt*).

In the moonstones (*candrakāntamaṇi*), there are sprouts (*utkandala*)—meaning shoots—that arise for the sake of nectar (*makaranda*), which is the production of water; these are pervaded by it, being merely reflected within the nectars. Thus, they "taste sweet," meaning they become dear to the people. //69//

He states the meaning established by the word *udaya* (arising) in the passage beginning with "it arises" (*udayati*), etc. By means of *tālas* in the form of throat-sounds, [he performs] *aṅgahāras*, which is to say, movements of the limbs; for it is by the sound of the *tāla* that dancers dance. [The flowers] have blossomed due to the arising [of the sound].
The bees approach the night-lotuses with a humming sound; thus there is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā).
Regarding the object "water," the term *karmāntika* means a laborer; that is to say, one who bestows nectar.
For those who speak much are indeed thirsty.
The eye, because it illuminates form, rises—that is, it pervades upward. //70//
"By them," and so forth. Even in the case of *timira* (a visual disorder), there is the attainment of omniscience because of the perception of the intended object.
"Abhisṛtāḥ" means "women going to meet their lovers" (*abhisārikāḥ*); this is according to [Pāṇini's rule] "roots meaning 'to go'... (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.167).
The past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is used in the sense of the agent for the root *smṛ*. In their eyes, [the flowers] were like "perfected collyrium" (*siddhāñjana*);
"perfected collyrium" refers to that which reveals hidden wealth and so forth.
It is a special kind of ointment that illuminates. For women going to meet their lovers (abhisārikās),
it is like blindness due to the absence of spreading [of vision] because of the fear of being seen by people in the moonlight.

In darkness, however, one may move about at will; thus, it possesses the quality of "perfected collyrium" (siddhāñjana). Elsewhere, for those who behold the three worlds, it acts as dense veils intended to blind them, because it obstructs the vision.
The word *vā* has the sense of "or" (*iva*) here; Amarasimha states, "The word *vā* is used in the senses of option and comparison.
By the phrase "washing away," he expresses the complete eradication of darkness.
*Sārvabhauma* means a king who is an *apratiratha* (unconquered in battle);
[the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the words *sarvabhūmi* and *pṛthivī* according to Pāṇini 4.1.85 (*sarvabhūmipṛthivībhyāmaṇañau*).
Due to its inclusion in the *anuśatikādi* group, there is vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) in both members of the compound.

Through the conquest of the enemy in the form of darkness that pervades the entire earth—favoring the wicked and suppressing the virtuous—he attained the status of a sovereign ruler of the whole world. //71//

He describes the experience of touching drops of nectar through the proximity of the moon by means of the cooling touch of snow, beginning with the words "In the world of the moon" (candraloka), etc. (173). Alliteration (*anuprāsa*) is the repetition of similar sounds; and that [repetition] is even more so than the preceding [instance].
It produces wonder;
as it has been said: "Alliteration (anuprāsa) is the repetition of phonemes within quarters and within words.
Regarding sweetness (*mādhurya*), the meaning is that [these sounds] are superior even to nectar. "Amūḥ" refers to those [sounds] such as those whose form belongs to the same class (*samānakula*).
They cause [them] to ascend to the supreme, most excellent state or station.

The meaning is that they gladden even more than nectar; and this is because the purpose of Sītā’s words is to convey that "being the object of a lover's affection alone is the supreme cause of excellence for women."
This is the ornament called *abhiprāya* (intention), because it manifests a sense of ownership (*mamatā*) toward Sītā;
as it has been said: "Others call *abhiprāya* a sense of ownership."
"In a pleasing object" (176). //72//

Having found an opportunity through such things as the movement of the *puṣpaka* chariot—difficult for humans to obtain—and the attainment of the world of the Moon (*candraloka*), he praises [the Lord] with the words beginning "Today" (*adya*), and so forth.

"Rubbing" (*gharṣaṇam*) refers to the shaking of the head born of joy. By means of "splendor" (*śriyā*)—that is, by light—which has been "cleansed" (*unmṛṣṭayā*), meaning rendered stainless, the darkness has been destroyed. By this, [he praises Him] in the music hall (*saṅgītaśālā*).
The concentration on the lamp has been described.
*Rava* means form; *vyāsaṅga* means obstacle.
By the "bull," that is, by the king; [there is] fame, having conquered Rāvaṇa.
"Having ascended the Puṣpaka chariot, he wanders through the world of the moon and other realms. By this, the pervasion of his fame throughout the netherworld (pātāla) is described. //73//
Through his skill in speech, he describes the pervasion of the heavenly realm with the words beginning "Bhogīndra":
*pramadottaraṅgam* means agitated by joy; *viṃśatiśatī* is a collective term for twenty hundreds (two thousand).
The compound is formed by the rule "taddhitārtha" (Pāṇini 2.1.51); the meaning is "two thousand," because [the serpent] has a thousand hoods. "With red [eyes]" means with sweet-sounding voices.

"Being ill-situated" means having an afflicted state. What indeed will he hear? He is simply incapable of hearing, because, like the rest [of the sense organs], his eyes lack the nature of being ears.
Existence. //74//
Rāma’s smile [was caused] by his acceptance of Vibhīṣaṇa’s praise;
[the passage beginning with] "It has begun," and so forth.
"Even when a rival—that is, a likeness—was being fashioned; that is to say, even when an attempt was being made to create a resemblance. [She was] obtained at the very moment of her birth;
[this was so] by bringing about the misfortune of her own creator and fashioner."
Self-betrayal (*ātmadroha*) arises from bringing about one's own deficiency. *Paryaṅka* means a seat;
it is the contraction of the lotus [of the heart] due to contact with the rays of the moon. The "craft" (*śilpa*) is the form of the moon; it is not "unopened" (*nonmīlita*).
It has been revealed; the sense is that the stain has not been wiped away. //75//
"By this," and so forth.
A *pratiyogin* (counter-correlate) is a measure (*māna*); those things such as *guñjā* seeds which have that nature are "counter-measures" (*pratimāna*). //76//
He says "having brought the lotuses" and so forth. "Born from a lotus" (*padmayoni*) is a statement regarding his lineage (*gotra*).

"Rising from bed" (*śayyotthāyam*) means having risen quickly from the bed; the suffix *ṇamul* is used here according to Pāṇini 3.4.51 (*apādāne parīpsāyām*). "The whole day" (*ahaḥ*) uses the accusative case for continuous duration (Pāṇini 2.3.5). [This refers to] in relation to a single object alone.
"Whose tip is the edge";
that is to say, inclined toward a single point. //77//

He speaks the words "Noble Lord" (*āryaputra*) to describe, even in a mere fraction, the smiling and downcast nature of her face caused by self-praise. The commentary (*chāyā*) says: "Noble Lord, how then?"
Did the Blessed Lord Bhūtanātha, disregarding such a full-orbed moon, make it his crest-jewel as if it were merely a single digit?
"How" (*katham*) means "for what purpose"?—this is the question. [The suffix] *thamu* is applied according to the rule *kimaśca* (Pāṇini 5.3.24).
"Of the three," and so forth. "Entire" (*samagram*) means a complete circle. "O dear one" (*aṅga*) is used as a form of address.
The fact that an offering of flowers (*nirmālya*) is no longer fit for consumption is expressed by: "My food offering (*naivedya*) is unworthy [of being consumed]; the leaf..."

From Līlāvalī’s statement, "Flowers, fruits, and water," [it follows that] "moreover," and so forth. When the Lord is the full moon, he is "measured by the month" (*māsena pramite*), meaning thoroughly measured; the sense is that when the month has waned, he himself also wanes.
