"This very [portion], being merely a fraction, is seen"—the word "by people" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Furthermore, it means that it should be maintained because it is imperishable. However, if the reading ends in the nominative case—*pramitaḥ* = *pramātumārabdhaḥ* ("begun to be measured")—then the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the beginning of an action and also denotes the agent (Pāṇini 3.4.71). [This refers to the moon] by virtue of its waxing and waning.
For this is indeed the lunar month; as it has been said: "They desire the lunar month to have the new moon (darśa) as its limit" (183). In this reading, the word *bhagavat* is absent.
"Amṛta," and so forth.
*Āgrayaṇa* is the name of a specific sacrifice performed when new grain is harvested; by that [sacrifice]...
The first meal is indicated;
and its status as the "first meal" is due to its being the first thing perceived of that which torments the world.
The half-circle of a firebrand-wheel for the fire of desire; that is to say, an inflamer of passion.
A key (*kuñcikā*) is a specific mechanism for opening a door-panel;
the meaning is "one who wards off the darkness at the onset of night. In the context of counting heroes:
"Kāmaḥ prathamo vīraḥ" (Desire is the first hero) is a line for the purpose of counting; for a line intended for the first count becomes curved.
"Pratirājaḥ" means the full moon; its "bījam" (seed) is the cause; therefore, it is one that bestows superior bliss. //78//
Chāyā: Noble son, those possessed of virtues shine anywhere they may be; however, those who are diminished climb to the very top—of this, the moon upon the crest of Śiva is the primary illustration.
"Exhausted" means devoid of qualities (*guṇa*). The word "head" (*śīrṣa*) refers to the highest position;

and ascending to that is for the sake of self-revelation. The meaning is that even though the full moon is independent, it is indeed renowned, whereas the digit (*kalā*), however, exists only by depending on Hara.
"O great Kṣatriya" means, in short, one who is partial toward virtue;
for those who are diligent are indeed lovers of virtue.
To avoid the consequence of [the argument] being devoid of merit, he says: "The embankment and the commencement," and so forth.
*Goṣpada* refers to a specific small measure; it is grammatically correct according to the rule: "*goṣpadaṃ sevitāsevitapramāṇeṣu*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.145).
The meaning is that he leaped over it without effort. [This is according to] Pāṇini 5.3.53 (*bhūtapūrve caraṭ*): regarding the unfathomable depth of the ocean in its state of fullness.

Because it is not seen, there is no fear for one who leaps across it; yet, because all the water has been displaced by the throwing of mountains for the sake of building a bridge, the resulting pits are clearly visible— how, then, can such a deep place be crossed?
Thus is its nature as a source of fear; for instance,
that which is difficult to overcome due to the greatness of fullness belongs to that very same [state] of the void and the destitute.

The dignity of the virtuous becomes even more unassailable— that is, beyond being disregarded; for the world honors one with prosperity, yet that same person, when poor, requires honor to avoid being perceived as an object of pity.
Similarly, the sense is that even the moon, because it has waned, has ascended the head of Hara for the sake of great honor; however, in the present context,
[the reference is to] a well and so forth.
There is a worldly saying: "If a vessel is full, it does not cause alarm; yet that very same vessel, if empty, causes alarm. //79//
He describes the moon’s meditative absorption at the king’s departure with the words beginning "prācīna" and so forth. *Cūḍam* means the summit.
By the *uḍubhiḥ* (stars), acting as agents, through their own *niryāsaiḥ* (exudations), that is, their radiances, and by their own essential nature (*nijasvarūpeṇa*), [the moon is adorned].

The handfuls of parched grain (*lājāñjali*) were offered as the *arghya* offering, because the light [of the moon] is comparable to water and the stars are comparable to parched grain. The *pādya* and other honors constitute the royal mode of reception. The prominence of the dark spot (*kalaṅka*) is due to the prominence of the light.
"Tuccha" means empty or hollow; [it refers to the moon] while it is still in the state of a sprout.
"The darkness born of night has been removed. Regarding the word *naiśika*:

by the rule "and from *niśā* and *pradoṣa*" (Pāṇini 4.3.18), the suffix *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava*). By this, it is shown that the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for conquering the enemy occurs precisely at the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
Having emerged from the reflection (*bimba*), it spreads out—that is, it pervades all around; this is a construction where the object functions as the agent (*karmakartari*).

In connection with the mention of the word *kalaṅka* (stain), he says "the king of beasts," and so forth. *Bhaṅgurāṇi* means crooked. There is fear of the deer because of the sight of the *kiṃśuka* buds, which resemble the claws of a deer. //81//

"Indoḥ," etc. The word *iva* is used in the sense of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). That which is perceived in the form of a spot [on the moon] is so because it has been extracted from its state as a spot.
The meaning is that the place ought to be empty; since the taker extracts [the object] from the middle itself, it is the middle alone that becomes empty. //82//
Under the guise of describing Rāmabhadra, [the author] states the pervasion of the moonlight across heaven and earth with the verse beginning "rodasī" and so forth.

By the word "kūpa" (well), the smallness [of the well] is indicated in comparison to the fourteen worlds pervaded by Rāma’s fame; for this very reason, there is the metaphor of the frog-form. How much [is it]?

"It shines!"—the meaning is that it shines only very slightly. "Since" (yat)—that is, for which reason he roars back; "we do not perceive that very reason," is the ellipsis; the sense is that this is because [the sun] is pervaded by both worlds alone. //83//
He states the cause of the blemish: "I know," and so forth.
The commentary: "I know [that I was] defeated by competing with the splendor of my noble son's fame."
Now, the Blessed One, marked by the hare, has maintained contact with a stain;
for even those who are defeated remain possessed of a stain.
"I know" is used in the sense of conjecture (*utprekṣā*).
In connection with the topic of fame, he says "with effort" (*sārambham*), etc. The commentary (*chāyā*) states: "with effort."

Who does not sing of you, the Lord of the Raghus, whose complexion possesses the luster of the waves of the Milk Ocean tossed up by the agitation of Mount Mandara when it was overturned by your arms marked with the Śrīvatsa; you who are as white as the radiance streaming from the orb of the moon as it shatters during the waning of the dark fortnight?
Fame.
"With effort" means with exertion. "Among the arms" means in the midst of the arms.
"Whirling" refers to Mount Mandara; for during the churning of the ocean, Viṣṇu’s arms served as the supporting rope for Mount Mandara.

This is well-known from the Purāṇas. By its agitation, the "surge" (laharī)—meaning the flow of waves—rises up, its upper and lower parts being inverted. Its "inner luster and purity" (garbhakāntinairmalya) is due to the fact that its center remains unimpaired.
Since it is experienced that the digits (kalās) are indeed waning day by day during the dark fortnight through the decrease of their light,
it is precisely those [digits] that are described as possessing an excellence of brilliance.

Regarding the phrase "in the dark fortnight" (*andhakārapakṣe*): this expression is used because, during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣe*), the subsequent portion of the moonlight arises immediately after the darkness. //84//
"Let there be haste," and so forth.
This elaborate description of the moon mentioned previously is a cause for delay that obstructs the arousal of haste; and by means of that—

It should be understood that the absence of longing for the subject of the consecration is due to a delay caused by attachment to something else, and by that, his *dhīrodātta* (noble and self-controlled) nature is indicated.
From here onwards: "How is it that the delighter of Añjanā urges me to hurry?"

The passage ending with "How does Añjanānandana hasten? is the structural element named *grathana* (the connection), because it serves as an introduction to the primary matter at hand, which is the form of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). As it has been said: "Grathana is the introduction to that."
Thus [it is said]. The word *tat* refers to the subject matter at hand (*prakṛtakārya*).
The term *mārutir* contains within it the reason for his swift coming and going; for this very reason, the word *katham* expresses wonder.
Chāyā: How is it that Añjanānandana is hurrying us?
Therefore, O Blessed Puṣpaka, descend;
let us travel by a path close to the earth.
"Let us go. Noble son, what indeed is this, which, upon the circle of the earth dark as a fresh rain-cloud,
is like a cluster of rays from the Kaustubha gem upon the chest of Madhumathana?"
Is it seen burning?
[The text] says "the chisel and the adze," etc.
It cuts—that is, it severs.
Regarding the phrase "wood and so forth": *tarku* means a carpenter's adze or a tool made of iron.

It is derived from the verbal root *kṛtī* (DhP 6.105), meaning "to cut," with the substitution [of the vowel] and the addition of the *uṇ* suffix according to the *uṇādi* rules (194); [the form is derived] from this very [root].
It is like the word *kartarī* [derived from the root *kṛt*], or like the word *siṃha* [derived from the root *hiṃs*];
it means "the chisel of that," or "that which is both he (the Lord) and the chisel."

It is written as *tanūkṛtam*, meaning "a workshop for crafts. The shortening of the vowel occurs because of the rule "vibhāṣā senā" (Pāṇini 2.4.25), which prescribes the neuter gender [for such compounds], thereby resulting in the short vowel. //85//
"Jyeṣṭhāmūlīyā," and so forth.
Jyeṣṭhāmūlīyā refers to the full moon day in the month of Kārttika.
The pilgrimage performed at the Puṣkara tīrtha dedicated to the goddess named Hiṅgulā,
and its status as being associated with the month of Jyeṣṭha, generally occurring during that month.
Because either of the two constellations, Jyeṣṭhā or Mūla, is occupied by the sun,
that sacred site (tīrtha) belongs to that month.

It is of great merit. As it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "The merit that arises from the gift of a Kapilā cow at the holy site of Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika—that merit one obtains by drinking the water from the feet of a Brahmin. (197) On that [day]...
The path was distressed by joyful female camels and *priyaka* trees;
according to Amara, "a forest track is a difficult road" (198).

Because of the absence of grass and water in the desert (*maru*), and due to the abundance of *śamī* trees—which are dear to camels—travelers, for the purpose of transporting their loads, disregarded oxen and other draft animals.
Only camels are led [there]. Regarding this, Bhallaṭa says: "These are those very [plants], half-grown again after being licked by unrestrained, fierce young camels..."
O fool, why do you vainly whirl the sacrificial pin in the windless desert merely to die? (199)
Thus [he] denies; he destroys the power of vision, the sense being that it is due to the abundance of mirages. By that very fact, there is a similarity with a desert.

As it was said in the second act: "The slopes of the wilderness, where the lapwings are silent due to the forest being matted with masses of flames from sun-stones playing in the intense contact with the radiance of the fierce sun... (200)
*Viṣvadrīcībhiḥ* means pervading [all directions] due to the absence of obstructions such as trees;
*prasnuvānāḥ* means sweating; *phenāyante* means they are foaming, i.e., they are vomiting forth foam (by Pāṇini 3.1.17: *phenācca*).
Thus it is said: "From boiling by means of heat produced by the sun's rays, bubbles arise. (86)
With a lion’s glance, he describes the southern direction—beginning with "O Queen, to the south," and so forth. *Māṇikyācala* is the Rohaṇa mountain. //87//
Chāyā: Where the swan Agastya, resembling a kāśa flower, moves about.
Lopāmudrā is the wife of Agastya. This is the second hermitage.
In comparison with the *daṇḍaka*; and he will say [later] by means of the passage beginning with "one's own hand" (202).
Regarding "a large vessel" (*bṛhatpātra*) and so forth: *pātra* refers to the space between the two banks; [as in the expression] "the near and far shores" (*pārāvāre*).

"Parārvācī tīre pātraṃ tadantaram" (The word *pātra* refers to the further and near banks, as well as the space between them), according to Amara. And as for the recipient: when a worthy recipient (*satpātra*) has arrived, the virtuous reveal their own wealth.

By the phrase "having expanded that samādhi," he expresses this: although the "Jar-born" (Agastya) was a vessel for only a small amount of water—referring to his own cause—he himself held a vast quantity of water;
thus, his spiritual power (*anubhāva*) is described. Therefore...

This is the statement regarding [the Lord] being worthy of propitiation. Here, "lineage" (*kula*) refers to the lineage of knowledge (*vidyā-santāna*). The particle *kila* indicates tradition (*aitihya*).
"Swelling" (*śopha*) is a particular kind of disease. (204) "The state of being a physician" (*bhiṣaktvam*).
Because it causes that destruction.
*Āśvīnam* means "to be traversed by a horse in one day";
[the suffix] *khañ* is applied according to the rule *aśvasyaikāhagamaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.19); [it is used] in all three genders as *āśvīnam*.
"That which is traversed by a horse in a single day," according to Amara (206).
[The path] is called "the downward path" because of the immobilization of the Vindhya mountains.
Just as the sun, though himself worthy of worship by the world, considers that person worthy of worship because he has benefited him while rising into the sky; so too [is it with the Buddha].
This is the meaning. //88//

"Drunk," and so forth. Stiffness and heaviness arise from the lack of effort to fly for a long time; that flying [attempt] stems from the timidity born of being unaccustomed to the absence of water. "Distraught" means powerless; for this very reason, they have fallen.
"Kaulīram" means pertaining to a crab (*karkaṭaka*). "Entering a hole" is due to its inability to endure wind, heat, and so forth.

"Lack of refuge" is due to the absence of water. Regarding the word "moment" (*kṣaṇam*): it is because at another moment, out of compassion, it emits water. In the case of a rash act (*sāhasa*), there is no passion (*rasa*)—that is, no affection; thus, it is not appropriate.
The remainder [of the verse]: "In this context, 'rashness' (sāhasa) refers to the undertaking of an object that is impossible to praise. //89//
In the realm of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), Kāma is the sovereign king. Regarding the phrase "about to rise" and so forth:
because of its moistness, it bears the impression of lac; this is its nature as an impression (*lipitva*).
Because it indicates the return of a woman going to meet her lover, who had fled out of fear of the sound of footsteps and was herself afraid of the *cakra* bird. //90//
"Of those things pertaining to pearls" (*mauktikīyānām*) means "of those things which have pearls as their cause.
For the remaining sense [of "pertaining to"], the suffix *cha* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.2.114: *vṛddhāc chaḥ*.
"Oyster shell," and so forth.
The oyster shell (*śuktikā*) stands in the place of the womb; its "interior" (*garbha*) is the space within it.
"Solidified" (*stambhitāḥ*) means brought to a state of density. For that which has fallen into the womb-receptacle...
Vigor (vīrya) undergoes the stages of the embryo, such as the *kalala*, *budbuda*, and *ghana*.
Births (*prasūtayaḥ*) mean those who are liberated;
the transition from lap to lap is to be viewed as delightful. In this regard:
For those who are liberated, there is only the mental affliction of a child. //91//
"Yuvati," and so forth.
*Karaka* means hailstone.
(210) The mention of its "solidity" is because its nature is to melt.
Because of the ripening of those meritorious deeds— which were produced by the drops of water from their breasts and resulted in mutual experience— their hands became steady. //92//
Chāyā: Noble son, the Blessed Ocean’s partiality toward Bhāgīrathī is due merely to the courtesy of her being his elder;
however, the outpouring of the entirety of his love is [directed toward you].
It is described as being like the Tāmraparṇī river itself, beautiful with pearl ornaments on all its limbs that are innate.
*Dākṣiṇya* (courtesy) is equanimity toward heroines; it is "being equal toward many."

Because it has been stated [in the scripture], "He is the Dakṣiṇa" (211); the mention of courtesy (*dākṣiṇya*) and affection (*sneha*) is due to their being characteristics of a lover; and it is also said:
"While sprinkling..."
"Causing the prosperity of the *mādhavī* creeper and the remainder of the *kunda* flowers to increase,
he appears to me like a lover through the union of affection and courtesy.
(212) Thus.
The mention of pearl ornaments serves as an *ālambana* (objective) ornament because it acts as an excitant (*uddīpaka*);
as it has been said: "The qualities of the object, its activities, its ornaments, and that which is neutral [are the excitants]."
"The sequence of intensification (uddīpana) is to be understood as fourfold. (213) Thus [it is said].
Regarding the phrase "laughing": Rāma’s laughter [implies] that men are fond of new lovers, [while] toward elder [wives...]
Because Sītā’s speech is intended solely to convey courtesy,
[he acts] by reflecting on her mental agitation, thinking, "She is distressed by a lack of confidence in me.
For this very reason...
With reference to the liberation from pride (*mānamocana*), he says "she delights," and so forth.
[The phrase] "by the wind coming from this mountain" implies that it exists as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*).
"Even though our beloved has committed an offense, we know him to be innocent, since you have become angry."

Thus, by these women who speak untruths— women whose knots of pride have been shattered by the wind of this [teaching] and who are easily appeased— the sense is that you should not give way to anger. Therefore...
Thus is the statement that "he causes delight. //93//
"His own hands," and so forth.
The "forepart" (prāgbhāga) is the hem (añcala); because it is spread out there, it is "upturned" (uttāna), meaning not deep. [As it is said: "The deep is upturned."
"Viparyaya means the opposite of that," according to Amara. For this very reason, there is the visibility of the *timi* fish;
[otherwise] there would be distress (*kleśa*) due to the absence of water. That ocean (*sindhu*);
by means of compassion—or perhaps by disgust—arising from the conquest of internal crocodiles and external grasper-demons.
According to Amarasimha, "jugupsā," "karuṇe," and "ghṛṇe" mean disgust.
(215) The meaning is "he vomited. "Etat" refers to the *daṇḍaka* meter about to be described;
it is called "aparam" (the other) in relation to the *rohaṇa* meter. (216)

He states [the following] as a digression: "The four oceans," and so forth. Regarding the word "to cause to drink": because it is praiseworthy to give water to one who is thirsty. Regarding the word "having purified": at the rising of Agastya, the water becomes clear; as it is said: "At the rising of the great-splendored Agastya, whose source is a jar, the waters became serene" (217). //95//
"Fixed," and so forth:
that ritual action in which there is an injunction such as "Drink water" (*apaḥ*) and "Eat" (*aśāna*),
is described in that manner.
The compound *ehīḍādayo’nyapadārthe* (Pāṇini 2.2.24) is formed according to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group; and that [act] is prescribed for eating and other such activities.
As it has been said: "Having first performed the *apośāna* rite, honoring the food and not disparaging it...

(220); the word "should eat" (*bhuñjīta*) is to be supplied. "The Lord of Sages" (*munīndra*) is the reason for the rule regarding eating. "Those who consider themselves food" (*bhaktammanyāni*) means those who think of themselves as food.
"Regarding *ātmamāne* [in Pāṇini 3.2.83], *khaś* [is added]; *kim api* means precisely without cause; the sense is that he has no intention of eating it.
In the phrase *dhruvam iva*, the word *iva*..."

This is used as a poetic embellishment (*vākyālaṅkāra*). It is thus imagined that trembling is appropriate because the worlds are devoted to the waters of the oceans, which serve as their ablution water. (222)

[This is] the state [of affairs]. Even all the worlds trembled; or rather, the construction may be: "Are those who consider themselves devoted [to him] anything else? The trembling was due to fear. "Something indeed"—that is, quite without cause; for they did not take into account the compassion arising from his state as a sage.
The state [of being]. (96) (223) "A seat for the sake of Dharma" means a royal throne.
"The supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of the sages" is because there is an absence of affliction by *rākṣasa* demons.
The meaning is that the wealth of asceticism increases.
From this point onward begins the "Description of the Daṇḍaka Forest" (224).
The final conclusion (*nirṇaya*) is a structural element (*aṅga*) consisting of the narration of what has been experienced;
as it is said: "The narration of what has been experienced is indeed the conclusion" (225).
[This refers to] Rāma’s bashful smile resulting from the praise of his own extraordinary prowess.
The golden deer is Mārīca. "How so?
expresses wonder regarding the speed of the celestial chariot. "We shall establish ourselves" refers to *samava-pra* (Pāṇini 3.1.226).
By these and other such words, there is the derision of Sugrīva, arising from the recollection of his fear of Rāvaṇa.
*Upahāra* means surrender; for those who are afraid indeed surrender [themselves] for the sake of protecting their own lives.
They offer goats and other animals to spirits, vetālas, and the like; the implication is that if Rāma were present,
Rāvaṇa would have been slain by him at that very moment.
*Viḍambaḍambaraḥ* means an abundance of imitation.

Regarding the passage beginning with *viśvāmitra*, etc.: by the word *api* in the phrase *mukhād api*, he expresses both an excess of affection for Rāma and the beauty of his face; this is indicated by the two qualifying adjectives.
It indicates two occasions for stringing the bow. What else? Who is greater even than this?

[Those who have been struck] by a single arrow— Please provide the full passage you would like me to translate. You have provided a fragment; once I have the complete text, I will provide the translation as requested.
The meaning is that you alone are superior even to Rāvaṇa and others; for this very reason, there is this salutation. //97//
Sītā’s shame arises from the recollection of her abduction by Rāvaṇa. Prasravaṇācala is Mālyavat.
"At night," and so forth.
"Pāṭava" means the power to dispel darkness; because of the abundance of the gems' luster even at night,
the crows move about with the perception that it is day, while the owls [move about] [with the perception that it is night].
And there is the state of being hidden.
"It is remembered"—this is a question posed by way of the tone. *Uccair vyadhuḥ* means they made it high;
this [refers to] the leaves... *mā*.
The sense is that it is with the intention of saying "let him bathe.
"Kautuka" refers to the desire to see Sītā's embarrassment. //98//
The *kapotahasta* (pigeon-hand gesture) consists of folded palms (*mukulitāñjali*).
As it is stated in the *Vṛttaratnāvalī*: "That is the *kapota* [gesture] where the two hands have their roots, tips, and sides joined together, used for salutation and addressing a teacher."
"Even when the limbs of discipline have been undertaken.
(227) Shadow: O Blessed Goddesses dwelling in Janasthāna, here is Jānakī, your attendant, bowing before you.
"Of this," and so forth. *Phalinī* is the *priyaṅgu* plant. (228) There is a maturity in the offense consisting of the gift, indicated by the smile which suggests loftiness.
He was provoked by the violation of the maiden’s vow—that is, her innocent restraint consisting of the inability to endure nail-marks and the like.
The "violation" occurred because a bud resembling a nail-mark was placed [upon her]; for young maidens do not tolerate such things as nail-wounds. This state of being "smiling" [is described].
Because of the consideration of Rāmabhadra’s skill in deception. //99//
Regarding "asmin" and so forth:
*kādambinī* means a mass of clouds (*meghamālā*). *Sthūlaṅkaraṇaḥ* means a carpenter (*vardhaka*);
the suffix *khyun* is applied by the rule beginning with "āḍhya" (Pāṇini 3.2.56). And this—

Because of its quality of being an excitant (*uddīpaka*); the word "api" (even) indicates a contradiction, meaning that it is contradictory for a cloud that does not rain to increase the water. Likewise, "me"—that is, me who am suffering—having seen [this].
"Even by those who are agitated"; this is the cause for budding and dancing, while "by those protected by you" is the cause for the absence of those [states]. For kinsmen indeed [cause] suffering.
They share [it] out. //100//
Wrath is grief.
Shadow: O King of Vimānas, be gracious! It blazes, yet it does not shatter my adamantine [heart].
My heart! Therefore, hasten in such a way that this streak of the Daṇḍaka forest may be bypassed— like a forest fire,
because it reminds one of former sufferings— for indeed, [it is] not a thunderbolt.
It causes to fall away;
*riñcholī* means a row (*āvalī*).
"Not other," and so forth.

*Kṣuṇṇam* means crushed or struck; the sense is that [he] possesses a fortune not shared by others, because he brings joy to both the stationary and the moving through the production of sprouts and so forth, and by awakening passion (*madana*). *Svedāmbu* is the water of perspiration born of sexual union (*rati*). The *makara* belongs to Smara (the God of Love); it is the form of his banner, or Smara himself is the *makara*. The state of being enjoyed by him belongs to the sweat.

Because passion is the cause of pleasure; for the sea-monster (makara) indeed sports in the water. "Having drunk" means having dried it up; that is to say, having removed the exhaustion born of passion.
For this very reason, once again—
There is an occasion of joy from the embrace of one who desires sexual union. The doubling of the horripilation results from both the embrace and the touch of the wind.
From this point until the end of the passage "the supreme light is resorted to" (231).
Because it consists of mutual conversation, it is called the limb known as *paribhāṣaṇa* (dialogue); as it has been said: "Dialogue (*paribhāṣā*) is mutual speech" (232). //101//
"Bibhratīm" and so forth. That [rhetorical style] in which the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) or the pathetic (*karuṇa*) sentiments are described through an extremely delicate composition is called *kaiśikī*.
As it has been said: "The *kaiśikī* is considered to be that whose meaning and composition are exceedingly delicate."

"The two [rasas], the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the pathetic (*karuṇa*), are considered to be extremely delicate" (233). Regarding this, *sandarbha* means composition or weaving (234). Of that—of the fragrance, namely the meaning consisting of the erotic and so forth—it is "emitting," that is, bestowing (235).

Speeches (giraḥ), characterized by such qualities as a delicate composition; bearing [them]; of that country, Vidarbha—meaning the Vaidarbha style. As it has been said: "Free from harshness of construction..."

"The Vaidarbha style is held to be free from harshness of sound and not characterized by excessively long compounds. (236) This was stated because *vṛttis* (meters) depend upon meaning, whereas *rītis* (styles) depend upon sound. "They attend" means they practice. //102//
The Andhra region is the country of Andhra.
"Saptagodāvara" is a collective term for seven Godāvarī rivers; even when referring to a single part of a river, the designation "river" is conventionally applied.
This is due to a metaphorical usage based on the fact that [the work] was composed by those respective sages;
the compound *godāvarīsaṃhitā* is an avyayībhāva formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.20 (*nadībhiśca*) in the sense of a collective; [and] "of the river Godāvarī and of a number..."
If [the word] *uttara* [is used], the suffix *ac* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.2.127]. That very thing is the *hāra* (necklace);
it is the central hero (*nāyaka*) because he stands in their midst.
"At that time," and so forth.

"At that time" means during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). By the word "ārabhaṭī," the dance called *tāṇḍava*, which is characterized by that particular mode of performance, is indicated. (239) [He is] one whose single foot remains—this being an *ekaśeṣa* compound meaning that only one foot is left as the other half has fallen away. Therefore...
Thus, bearing that body which consists of the southern half-measure— terrible (*bhairava*), awe-inspiring, and known by the name Bhairava— for at the time of dissolution,
both halves of the Lord of Half-Woman (*Ardhanārīśvara*) possess my own skill in the matter of dance.
Thinking, "I alone possess skill," they disagreed with one another out of pride and separated, each becoming a witness to the other's dancing.
Let them dance in turn.

Herein is the praise of Śaṅkarācārya: "Of the Lord, the Supreme Bhairava, whose body is severed and who has performed the Tāṇḍava dance at the destructions at the end of the aeons, [there is] she (the Goddess) who possesses the noose, the goad, the sugarcane bow, and the flower-arrows."
"Your single form alone is the witness. (240) In that regard,
when the southern portion called *cidambara* [unites with] the left portion called the Mistress of the Seven Crores (*saptakoṭīśvarī*),...
In the matter of dancing, he excelled; then, by mutual agreement, the right [hand] was withdrawn into itself by the left;
at that very moment, there arose two mantras named after them, consisting of ten and eight syllables respectively.

"Thus [they] have been revealed"— in this regard, the context of the *Mahātantra-āgama* should be investigated. (241) "The one-footed and the one of terrible form" refers to the deities within the enclosure of Aghora.
It is well known that the form of Bhairava has only one leg.
(242) "Tulyam" means at one time;
because Vāsuki had been emaciated by dancing, he was reduced to nothing but bones.
The Lord is adorned by two serpents that feed on bones according to the *tantra* [of his power].
Regarding the word "karmānta": *antaḥ* means intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*); thus, *karmāntaḥ* refers to one whose intrinsic nature is action.
The suffix *ṭhan* (Pāṇini 5.2.115) is applied because he possesses this [nature], meaning "one who destroys" (*saṃhartā*).

He describes the dance itself with the words "at the commencement of the dance," and so forth. *Rasāt* means from passion (*anurāga*), which is centered on the Lord (*īśvara*); [the phrase] *trasantyeva śivayā* is a compound according to the rule for *mayūravyaṃsaka* and similar formations (Pāṇini 2.1.72). Of his own empty half...

For the sake of fulfillment— that is, for completion— [he is] one by whom the "sport" (vibhrama)— meaning the whirl— the nature of which is rotation, has been "carried out to its conclusion," i.e., brought to its end; [to him] by means of that whirling.

Like the wheel of a firebrand produced by Pūraṇa, such [a state] is incomparable (245). To a person who has ceased from wandering, as if they themselves were wandering, even the directions appear as if they are spinning.

Such is the experience. I do not believe it; for even after one has ceased dancing, because of the eyes whirling due to the residual momentum (*saṃskāra*) of the previous spinning, one perceives Vāsuki and others as having completed the dance.
The meaning is that it was not ascertained. //104//

He describes the Goddess’s role as a witness to the dance with the words beginning "krīḍā" (play), etc. "Nipīte" means rendered invisible due to similarity [of color] and "chinne" (cut); by this, he alludes to the incarnation known as Chinnamastā. (246)
"Kālakaṇṭhī" contains within it the reason for her invisibility.
"Kālarātri" is the power (śakti) that destroys; she dances as if separately upon the head of the headless trunk (kabandha).
The phrase "asambaddhe" (in the unconnected) means that one should behold [the deity] out of fear; however,
in the *Chinnamastāvatāra*,
there is indeed a separate dance in reality, and here too [it is the same].

Praise of Śaṅkara: Victory to you, O Conqueror of Death, who are extolled by the crests of all the Vedas; you who, in the dances at the end of the great aeons, playfully severed your own head! (247) //105//
"Perspiration," and so forth.
"Picchilābhiḥ" means "lubricated"; the suffix *ilac* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *piccha*.
Even though there is looseness due to perspiration born of exhaustion from sexual union, [there is firmness] of the embrace.

The sudden firmness [of her body] due to the quivering pillars of horripilation born from the awakening of desire indicates the uninterrupted state of her passion (rati), and by that, the abundance of excitants (uddīpana) for the city [of the body] is suggested. //106//
"Abhimukha," and so forth.

"Patayālubhiḥ" means those having the nature of falling (*patanaśīlaiḥ*); the suffix *āluc* is applied in the sense of habitual tendency (*tācchīlya*) according to the rule "spṛhi-gṛhi" (Pāṇini 3.2.158); and this [falling] is due to their being face-downward.
*Puruṣāyitam* means acting like a man; that is to say, sexual intercourse with the woman on top. [The mention of] perspiration and weakness is due to the excessive exertion.
"She tells" means she indicates. //107//
The deity of love is Kāma; the inner sanctum is the place of residence;
the region is the domain;
"of the lover," and so forth.
Of fair-limbed women approaching their lovers,
[this was done] for the purpose of not being seen while going to meet them during moonlit nights.
Of those wearing white ornaments,
who were flying up as if traveling through the sky— the root *ḍīṅ* meaning "to go through the air"—
their shadows (*chāyā*) were devoid of sunlight (*anātapa*).
Only the location is perceived, not the intrinsic nature, due to similarity; the sense is that it is like milk in a conch shell. //108//
"Below," and so forth.
"Of those moving" means of those eating; [the root] *car* is used in the senses of "motion" and "eating.
(252) The essence of the moonlight itself is the oil (*sneha*); of that...
A small leather vessel is a *kutupa*; under the governing rule "for short [stems]" (Pāṇini 4.1.25), [the suffix] *ḍupac* is applied after *kutu*, resulting in *kutūḥ*.
According to Amara, "kṛtti" means skin, "sneha" means oil, and "pātra" means a vessel; thus, "kutupa" is a small leather oil-vessel.
[The crane] has an upturned beak for the purpose of drinking.
Because they have drunk the essence of moonlight up to their necks and because their bellies are distended from that consumption, they resemble ghosts (*kutapa*);
those staying on the palace rooftops gaze upon [the scene], for the destruction of darkness results from the entry of the moonlight. //109//
"Here," and so forth.
"Satiated" means satisfied; for that very reason, he is a "tundaparimṛjaḥ," one who rubs his belly, which is to say, lazy.
For those who are satiated wipe their bellies; this is for the sake of laziness,
according to the rule "in the case of *tuṇḍa* and *śoka*."
The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule *parimṛjāpanudoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.5). For this very reason, he is "one who has slightly enjoyed the moonlight" (*iṣadbhuktacandrikaḥ*).
Because of drinking the splendor of the woman’s face, there is a lack of regard for the moonlight; thus, this is a hyperbolic description (*atiśayokti*) of the excellence of her facial radiance.
In the compound *bhuktābhuktā*, the formation is a *nañ-viśiṣṭa* (negation-qualified) compound according to the rule *ktena nañviśiṣṭenānañ* (Pāṇini 2.1.60). //110//

A branch-city (*śākhānagara*) is a city immediately following the principal city; as Amara states: "Any other city that is distinct from the root-city is a branch-city" (258). Regarding the phrase beginning with *tripura*: the meaning is that he stood here and burned the cities.
"Uddāma," and so forth. *Bhrami* is that which constitutes the limbs of the cosmic dance (*tāṇḍava*) at the end of an eon (*kalpānta*);

by it, they are "shattered," meaning their joints and bonds have fallen apart. For this very reason, the matted locks (*jaṭā*) themselves are "expanded," meaning long, and are thus "channels" (*praṇāḍyaḥ*), or waterways. [The word] "of the two" (*dvayoḥ*)...
"Pranāḍī means the path of milk," according to Amara; [the rays] flowing forth from them.
The "staffs of Ganges-water" are streams; these themselves are the "staffs of the cage.
Having constructed that world-renowned cage, which was encircled—that is, surrounded—by them; for a cage is indeed surrounded by staffs.

In the midst of that, becoming himself a female swan (haṃsī), he is like an actor in the performance of a *nāṭikā*—a minor dramatic form—of "decay" (*vyaya*) itself, meaning destruction; that is to say, he is the destroyer of the world. //111//
"Namaḥ" and so forth.
"Praṇālī" means a stream, used here in a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇayā*). "Snaptitau" means they have been bathed; that is to say, they have been illuminated.
"Svāhākṛtam" means offered as an oblation (*hutam*). "Of that world," refers to its "prasavam," which is its origin (*utpattim*).
"To one who has offered oblations" means to one who has cast [the seed] into the fire; this expression is used because desire (*kāma*) is the seed for the production of the world.
Regarding the phrase "conquered by Smara," it should be understood that [the subject] was not born from a womb. //112//
"Vegāt," and so forth.
"Jaḍaḥ" means devoid of comprehension; the sense is that he became incapable of burning.
"Jāḍyam" (stupefaction) is a transitory mental state (*sañcāribhāva*). //113//
Chāyā: Oh, even for the venerable Lord whose crest is the moon—who has swallowed the fourteen worlds—his hunger for eyes has not fled, since even Madana has been made his prey!
"Became an arrow," and so forth. "With the hope of sustenance" means with the desire for support.
When [the enemy] had fled or retreated; by reason of his virtue;
"one who has drawn the bow" and "one who has discharged the weapon"—this is a *karmadhāraya* compound; regarding the states of bending and rising [of the bow], from Garuḍa...

Due to fear and the possibility of failure, the exertion— meaning the effort— is limited by the joining [of the arrow]; for since the drawing and the release of the bowstring are accomplished spontaneously, [the effort] consists merely in the joining of the arrow.
The meaning is that this is the effort of the Lord. //114//
*Khalacurī* is a specific lineage; therein dwell the *narendras*, descendants of the lineage of Kārtavīrya.
"Āśleṣā," and so forth.
The bodiless one (Anaṅga) acts as a guarantor because he provides the stakes for the embrace and other acts;
although that stake consists of enjoyment, the meaning is that even when there is no difference in the results of victory or defeat, [the same applies] to both the young woman and the youth.
"Of the two youths"; [this is] a singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) according to the rule "A male [remains] with a female" (Pāṇini 1.2.67).
"Only to conquer"—the sense is that even mere defeat brings about distress. //115//
"Of the Goddess," and so forth.
*Maṣī* is like ink, because of its blackness. *Sindhoḥ* means of the Mandākinī.
*Sadhrīcī* means a companion (*sahacarī*); [this is derived] from the rule "for *saha*, [the substitute] *sadhrī*" (Pāṇini 6.3.95). [She is] one whose love is unceasing.

Thus it was: the Lord of the Ancestors (Pitṛpati), namely Yama, having forcibly seized them—that is, having taken them away—[attained] the state of being free from the affliction of the setting sun upon reaching the [celestial] sphere, by way of metaphorical designation as a door to gradual liberation;
those dwelling on the banks of the Yamunā were liberated.
The meaning is that they come into being. (263)//116//
"Tripuretyādi": [The compound] "kirīṭe krīḍitāni yeṣām tāni" is a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* (a possessive compound with non-co-referential members);
or alternatively, it is a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Precisely for this reason...
Her friendship with the children arises from her association with the goddesses. She belongs to the ocean;
that is to say, she is his wife. //117//
"Gaurī," and so forth.

The crowding of Hara’s head is due to his half being divided by Gaurī, his co-wife, who is unable to bear [the weight] because of her river-like nature; for this very reason, it is only a single portion of the head.
Through the stability of the entire flood of water, its depth has doubled; it also suggests that even though Gaurī’s rivalry was made manifest, she herself remained profoundly deep. //118//
"Of the god," and so forth.

*Āgāmukā* means "arrived"; [the suffix] *ukañ* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.154 (*laṣapatapada...*), and the prohibition of the genitive case is applied according to Pāṇini 2.3.69 (*na lokā...*). *Itaḥ* means "on its own bank."

"Udyātān" means those that have gone upward; for this very reason, "pratīpān" means moving against [the current], going upstream. "Drāk" means quickly. There is an even more intense velocity even in the current.
Even from descending with excessive speed, [one reaches] the world of Brahmā, because one has come from that very place. //119//
Chāyā: This Mandākinī, which has bound the three worlds together by its own current, pays homage.
"Bound" (sandānita) means tied. The meaning is that she prevents the three worlds from falling by her own greatness.
"Dhanādhinātha," and so forth. *Praṇaya* means a request. (267) By the word *niketana*, "dwelling" (*nivāsa*) is indicated. Because of Kubera’s request, his dwelling is on Kailāsa;
however, since [Śiva’s] love is for this very place, the word *purī* ("city") is employed. //120//

"By those floating," and so forth. "Floating" means subject to birth and death. "Island" (dvīpa) refers to land in the midst of water; it is analyzed etymologically as "a place where waters have gone in two directions" (dvidhā gatā āpo 'tra).
By the rules "after *dvi*, *antara*, and prepositions, *ap* becomes *ī*" (Pāṇini 6.3.97) and "in the case of *ṛc*, *pūḥ*, etc. (Pāṇini 5.4.74), the suffix *ap* is elided.
Just as reaching the further shore is difficult when there is no island for rest, so too [is it difficult]...
The implication is that liberation occurs even in the absence of residing in Vārāṇasī. //121//

Regarding the passage beginning with "the shadow of the throat" (*kaṇṭhacchāyā*) and so forth: by the rule *vibhāṣā senā* (Pāṇini 2.4.25), the word *chāyā* may optionally take the neuter gender. Because the coils of the black serpent—which serve as the place for her necklace—are obscured by the luster of her throat, Pārvatī remains fearless, seeing only the jewels upon its hoods.

The Sāma melodies possess a more subdued tone because, due to the severed head having no connection with the trunk, they do not proceed from the *mūlādhāra* but instead emerge from the throat alone. //122//
"Navonmīlat... and so forth.
"Kimapi" means that his intention to press [her] was not understood.
He proceeded; [the meaning is that he began].

The word "pīḍane" (in the act of afflicting) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. In that context, "compassionateness" [is required] because of the absence of harshness; "having fulfilled one's purpose" [occurs] even in the absence of affliction caused by oneself.
Because she was the recipient of Sītā’s marriage, which was equal to a self-chosen embrace;
she captivates [the mind],
being fixed upon the eyes through both her beauty and familiarity.
The meaning is that it comes into being. //123//
Chāyā: Mother Mithilā, you are worthy of my salutation. Please convey my salutations even to my elders.
For one who is giving birth—that is, for one who is in labor—every year... [samāṃ samām]

Regarding the word *vijāyate*, the *Kāśikā* states: "In this context, they say that the root *jan-* occurs in the sense of 'delivering a fetus. *Ariṣṭamandira* means a maternity chamber; Amara says, "*Ariṣṭa* is a maternity chamber. It is, therefore, the place of Jānakī’s birth.
Up to this point:
"pāṃsukrīḍā" (playing with dust) has been explained as it was previously stated; by that [activity], she is a "sakhi" (companion); the meaning is "childhood companion."

By the term "playing in the dust," childhood play is indicated; the meaning is that his heroism was attained precisely through such childhood play by breaking the bow of Ajagava and the bow of Bhārgava.
Regarding Rāma's bashful smile due to his own praise: "by modesty," and so forth; by modesty as the cause, and with sweet words, meaning pleasing ones.
She is delightful through her graceful charms (*vilāsa*); she is beloved because of her lack of vulgarity (*agrāmyatva*).
For this very reason, [the following applies].

The *kaumāravratam* is the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*); its practice is like a penance grove (*tapovana*). For a penance grove is generally characterized by self-restraint. The intended meaning is that the heroines and heroes here are of the highest class.
He expresses this very point with the words beginning "with horripilation" (*romāñca*), etc. "Heaving" (*ucchvasantaḥ*) means full or swelling, due to being overcome by bliss.

Even when an embrace is slack, its firmness is restored by the sighing at the end; by the plural number, he indicates the manifold variety of embraces. "Having made it residual" means having left only a small portion remaining.

Having done so; likewise, having burnt— that is, having consumed— the wick, which is the lamp-cord, located on the staff— that is, situated upon the support of the staff— meaning, situated in the middle of the *mallikā* flower.
Or when the oil particles contained within the parts of a jasmine flower, resting upon a support in the form of a stick,
are set ablaze, the darkness does not reach even to the height of one's navel within the houses.
It covers [the body] because,
by remaining within the lamp's bowl, it obstructs its edge; thus, the darkness does not reach the height of the navel, and for that reason, the lower part of the body is not seen.
That which comes into being is a "state" (*bhāva*). At that time, they display their innate, secret cleverness—that is, their skill in sexual union.

These women are of the "middle" (*madhyā*) type, because of their equal measure of shame and passion. (274) This is stated regarding those present there during the fourth watch by way of a description of sexual enjoyment.
He speaks of the state of being a *padminī*; as it has been said: "In the fourth watch of the night, she delights the *padminī* among women. (275) //124//

The "earth-gods" are the Brahmins; "the primary abode" means that they dwell there precisely because of its merit. "Within the sacrificial altar" (*antarvedi*) refers to the region between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers.
"To the east" (*pūrveṇa*) means in a place not far from the eastern direction; [this is according to the rule] *enapā*.
The second [verse] begins with "kṛṣṇāguru" and so forth; this is stated because of the blackness of the Kālindī and the whiteness of the Gaṅgā.
They meet together; that is to say, at the sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Prayāga.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Himālaya":
*pāṇḍu* means white; *kālī* means black.
The words "Himalayan" and "midday sun" [respectively] contain within them the causes for the coldness and the darkness of the two rivers. //125//
"Balī" and so forth: "at every step" means at every place of the enemy of Bali, namely Hari.

From the Brahma-maṇḍala, to the foot of Viṣṇu, then to the crest of Hara, and from there falling upon the Himavat; thus, by the whiteness of the rays of the nails resting on each of those [locations], there is an increase in the white luster of the river. Hence, she is called "Vaibudhasaindhavī" (the celestial river).
By the rule "hṛdbhaga" (Pāṇini 7.3.19), there is vṛddhi for both members of the compound; [as for the meaning], Amarasimha states: "Gaṅgā, Viṣṇupadī, Jahnutanayā, and Suranimnagā. //126//
"Prayāga," and so forth.

*Uccaistarām* means "most excellent" (*uttamam*) and also suggests "highest" (*unnatatamam*). The suffix *ām* is added to the form ending in *tarap* by the rule *kimettiṅavyayaghād ām* (Pāṇini 5.4.11). Although excellence as a substance (*dravyaprakarṣa*) is present here, it is not [expressed].
It is intended [to mean]:
"In grammar, it is not merely the actual existence of a thing that is the cause [of its being expressed], but rather intention as well."

The Commentator [states]: (280) That which is called "saṃsāra" is the stream of birth and death. Its "far shore" (*paraṃ pāram*) is non-rebirth; it is also [referred to as] the "opposite bank" (*aparataṭam*).
It throbs; it is perceived—that is, it is experienced and seen—and thus they become liberated.
This is also a meditative absorption (samādhi) by which even an extremely distant place is seen by one situated on a high vantage point.
It throbs. //127//
"Truly indeed," and so forth;
"the door to liberation" refers to the Gaṅgā and Yamunā as the gateway to the deity in all forms of worship.
Because of their proximity; [the two rivers] which, standing on both sides of that gate, bear—that is, convey—the splendor [of the city]. //128//
"Śyāma," and so forth.

Regarding "chāyām": by the rule *upānvadhyāṅvasaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.48), the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) receives the designation of object (*karman*); [and] by the rule *vaseḥ tavyat kartari ṇicca* (Vārttika 1 on Pāṇini 3.1.97), the suffix *tavyat* is applied with the augment *ṇic* in the sense of the agent.
The word "api" (even) indicates a contradiction:

[the idea] that even those situated in shadow practice the light. Precisely for this reason, there is the quality of being a marvelous feat. Herein, because the direct realization of Brahman occurs, there is no contradiction. //129//
Regarding the phrase "the sprout of the sacrificial post" (*yūpāṅkura*) and so forth:
by the word "sprout," he precludes the possibility of destruction, as would apply to something dry like a withered stump.
"Being counted" means that the number [of items] is known by means of the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) in the sacrifice. "Of the queen" (*mahiṣyāḥ*) refers to the principal wife;
"in the station" (*pade*) means within the sphere of her authority; "of the turban" (*paṭṭasya*).

She whose splendor is like that of [an image] fashioned from gold and other precious materials; for a queen indeed receives the binding of the turban, as it is said: "A consecrated queen is a *mahiṣī*. (284)
Thus ends Amara [Kośa], verse 130.
"Sky-like," and so forth:
"upturned" because they are seen directed upwards; "broad" or "vast" because of the intensity of their gaze; "motionless."
Because he is possessed by wonder due to the slaying of Rāvaṇa and others, the perception of a "forest in the sky" is a marvel.

From this point until the end of verse 285, "Rāmabhadra [appears] again on the path of vision," it constitutes the structural element (*aṅga*) named *upagūhana* (embracing), as it consists of the attainment of wonder.
As it has been said: "The attainment of the marvelous through the perception of effects occurs when one is enveloped by a prior state of being. (286) //131//
"By stalks," and so forth.
*Vṛnta* means the stalk that binds the flower; "the stalk is the binding of the blossom," according to Amara (287). This describes the similarity of the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) to stalks.
[She is so called] because of the relationship characterized by the nature of means and end through the succession of sacrificial fruits such as heaven;
she is "sweet" (*madhurām*), meaning beloved because she possesses all objects of enjoyment in abundance.

And "endowed with sweet flavor"; according to Amara, "the words *madhura* and *priya* mean 'sweet'. [He attained] *siddhi*, which consists in being the bestower of grace upon Indra and others through victory over the Rākṣasas who were preeminent in their powers of illusion (*māyā*).

The instrumental case in "yūpaiḥ" (with sacrificial posts) functions as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). By the mention of its sweetness, it is stated that Ayodhyā itself possesses the fruit of a thousand sacrifices;

by that, it is expressed that [Ayodhyā] is distinguished by all the happiness established in all worlds, such as heaven, which is accomplished through numerous sacrifices. That which is sweet and connected to the stalk (*vṛnta*) is precisely that.
This is the result: by this [means], heaven and so forth become objects of enjoyment for the city,
and from Indra [comes] the valor of kings.
And thus, his superiority in neutralizing the illusions of the Rākṣasas has been indicated. For this very reason, it was said that he did not find it pleasing;
the sense is that it was inferior because it was something to be overcome.
The dative case is used by virtue of the rule beginning with "rucyarthānām" (Pāṇini 1.4.33). //132//
He states the reason for this distinction with the words "such as these" (*tādṛśāḥ*) and so forth.

"Such as these" means those whose bonds placed by the gods had been removed; that is to say, they were heroes. By the phrase "were born in former times," he expresses his own humility, implying: "I am inferior to them in the present day."

It reveals [the rule for] the *aindrābārhaspatya* offering, meaning that which has those two as its deities (*tad-devatāka*); the suffix *ṇya* is applied by the rule "after *ditya*, *aditya*, etc. (Pāṇini 4.1.85), and the vṛddhi strengthening of both members of the compound occurs by the rule "in a *dvandva* of deities" (Pāṇini 7.3.21).

*Vaibhava* means power. For the fruit of this *caru* offering is its priceless nature and valor; and thus it is heard in the section beginning: "The gods were indeed afraid of the Rājanya being born" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.4.1).
By this, he indicates the entrance of Vasiṣṭha. //133//

The "requisites" (*sambhāra*) for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) are the ritual implements (*upakaraṇa*), such as the wheel (*cakra*) and so forth. "For us" (*naḥ*) means for ourselves; "it does not cause wonder" (*na citrīyate*) means it does not produce astonishment. [This is explained] by the rule beginning with *namovariva* (Pāṇini 5.1.294).

The suffix *kyac* is applied in the sense of "causing wonder" (*āścaryakaraṇe*); because the marker *ṅ* is attached in the rule *citraṅ*, the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) ending is used according to the rule *anudāttaṅitaḥ*. *Piṇyāka* refers to crushed sesame seeds from which the oil has been extracted; and this [is an example] of that which consists of excellence produced by the power of asceticism (*tapas*).
Because Rāma has carried away the nectar; since Bhārgava, who was victorious over Rāvaṇa and Kārtavīrya even in his childhood, has now been defeated,
therefore at this time—
The meaning is that even the slaying of Rāvaṇa, though he was the lord of the three worlds, is not a cause for wonder. //134//
"By arrows," and so forth;
in the form of the *pīṭha*, at the boundary— that is, the limit—
it is completed, meaning fully perfected.
He whose section or chapter consists of action in the form of battle— since the purpose of his incarnation was precisely the slaying of Rāvaṇa—
and who is characterized by fame associated with victory and auspiciousness.
"In the path of the eyes"; the word "exists" (vartate) is to be supplied. "Diṣṭyā" is an indeclinable used in the sense of joy;
it means "we are delighted. As it is said: "Diṣṭyā and samupajoṣam are used in the sense of joy" (Amara-kośa 3.3.247).
Thus ends Amara [Kośa], verse 135.

"Raghu," and so forth. *Brahmakriyā* refers to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). He was the foremost among those proficient in the Vedāntas. *Brahmarṣi* means a sage who is a creator of the world.
From this point until the end of verse 298, "the Ikṣvāku lineage has been favored," [the text describes his lineage].
Because it consists of the attainment of the increase of one's entire desired lineage, it is the limb named *ānanda* (bliss);
as it has been said: "Bliss is the attainment of what is desired. //136//
"Having taken," and so forth.

Herein lies the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) on the refining, massing, and spreading of the color of impure fragments of silver. The cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) itself is the crucible (*mūṣā*), for the purpose of melting and turning.

A clay vessel; according to Amarasimha, "tejasāvartanī" means a crucible. Having placed [the substance] within that, [one should consider] obstacles—those brought about by fate and those employed by adversaries—as follows:

It would not be so; for by "dhamatā" is meant heating, and by "tejas" is meant prowess. Precisely because of this, "guṇa" refers to both color and qualities such as valor, and [the fire] possesses excellence therein. "Piṇḍastham" means that which has become solidified, yet it also pervades the entire world.
Alkali is an impurity of iron that obstructs its brilliance; in the present context, it refers to causing public revulsion.
[The mind] is like silver free from that [impurity].

According to the *Amaraśeṣa* (301), "silver is [called] *tāra* when its color is free from impurities. For example, just as silver, when purified by heating (*āvartana*), becomes free from defects of color such as tarnish; so too [is the case here].

It becomes condensed and expanded in the form of gross objects and so forth; likewise, because it was attained through the victory of the famous ones such as Rāvaṇa, it is as if composed of their fame— condensed and pervading all the worlds.

The meaning is that he has obtained stainless fame, because it is free from the defect known as "bitterness" (kṣāra), which consists in causing distress to the world, owing to its quality of bringing joy to all the worlds. //137//
"Trijagad," etc.: "In leaping" means in reaching; "by those who travel on foot" means by those who are swift; that is to say, by those who pervade the three worlds.
And this, as well as the quality of sanctity, is the reason for the similarity with the Gaṅgā.
The indeclinable *atīva* is an indivisible particle used in the sense of excess; Amarasimha states: "The words *su*, *ati*, and *iva* are used in the sense of intensity" (302).
Your royal glories were already pure even before, but by your majesty they have become exceedingly so.
That is to say, she has become worthy of the world's respect. //138//
Even though his unsurpassed fame and the excellence of his lineage were already established, he says "jagat... and so forth, expressing the hope for the attainment of a son.
[The word] *āloke* means "in illumination," that is to say, in making manifest; *dhaureyau* means "capable. This is because of their protection of the family.
"Produce equality with the arms of Rāma;
by this, he expresses his hope for superhuman power even for those yet to be born. //139//
By the statement "it is indeed common," he indicates that the birth of offspring occurs only in Sītā;
"amhahe" is an expression signifying joy.
The particle *nipāta* is used in the sense of "by good fortune" (*diṣṭyā*). Example:
"By good fortune, my noble husband is free from co-wives."
He will become a householder;
Lakṣmaṇa’s path will transcend [ordinary] blessings because, even while in human form, he acts as a protector of the gods.
He says that very thing: "the hero," and so forth. The designation "Indrajit" contains a reason that illuminates his nature as a protector (*rakṣas*). *Dakṣiṇā* means a gift to be given;
one who is worthy of that is *dakṣiṇīya*.
"And from the gift of chaff" (303);
that is to say, [even] a vessel for the granting of fearlessness. //140//
"Nevertheless," and so forth.

The "first king" is Manu; his "lineage" (*vaṃśa*) refers to his family (*kula*), and also to a bamboo cane (*veṇu*). For a bamboo cane possesses many branches; by the comparison with a lineage, the family is intended.
He describes the increase of sons, grandsons, and so forth. //141//
"O Noble One," and so forth. Regarding "the inner chamber of the palace": the point is that there is not even entry into the house, let alone the enjoyment of sovereignty.

From "starting from here" (*ita ārabhya*) up to "they act as is appropriate" (*yathocitam ācaranti*), there is the dramatic element named *prasāda* (favor/grace), which consists of mutual attendance; as it has been said: "Favor is attendance."
"His own self," and so forth:
the pillar's "plumpness" is perceived through its thickness due to being densely packed with a mass of *bindu*s; however, this [person] has limbs blooming with joy.
He is the brother of the Kaustubha gem as well, because that too was born from the ocean. //142//
Chāyā: My dear Bharata, like a cluster of lotuses kissed by the mass of the sun's rays,
may you long experience joy.
"O child," and so forth;
"for a long time with longing"; the plural number in "among the sandalwood trees" [is used].
This indicates other objects as well;
that is to say, even from sound, touch, and so forth, the satisfaction of all your senses comes only from the limbs of Rāmabhadra. //143//
"Like a sacrificial post, a sacrificial post"— meaning a pillar of edicts.
By using the word "sacrificial post," he expresses that the merit of such a work is equal to that of a sacrifice.
"Of the moon as well," and so forth.
"A row" (paṅkti) means a line; the meaning is that it is established in the form of arms.
"The arms of the same womb" (sodarabhujāḥ) means, in other words, as refreshing as the rays of the moon. //144//
"Even unworthy of being a servant to a servant"—this is the discipline [of humility]. "By his appearance," and so forth;
the meaning is that he is perceived as being like Lakṣmaṇa due to the similarity of their physical forms.
He says that very thing with the words "this" and so forth.
*Saṃvāvadūkam* means concordant (*saṃvādi*). A hand that is like a bolt is a *karārgalam*; this is a compound according to the *vyāghrādi* group. (306)
By means of the two words "eva," he expresses absolute similarity. //145//
Chāyā: My child,
become like Lakṣmaṇa through deeds that possess the gravity of extracting the thorn of sorrow from all the world.
The meaning is: "May you also, like Lakṣmaṇa, become a benefactor to the gods by slaying the Rākṣasas.
Chāyā: "Dear Śatrughna, where are the noble ladies?"
Regarding the word *kṛta*: here, *maṅgalācāra* refers to the auspicious rites connected with entering the house, such as the worship of the household deities (*gṛhadevatā*) and so forth.
"Madhyamāmbā’s residence"— the sense is that it was for the purpose of allaying her distress.
"Long-lived ones," and so forth— the sense is that even the service due to Bharata, which ought to have been performed by us, has been performed by you alone.
"Proper conduct," such as salutation and returning the greeting;
"rising again" means being born again. By this, he expresses the difficulty of Rāvaṇa’s victory.

From "beginning from here" up to "it will proceed for the sake of satisfaction" (307), there is a limb named *samaya*, which consists of the emergence from suffering; as it has been said: "The *samaya*..."
"Exit from suffering" (308).
"The Conqueror," and so forth.
This narrative, ending with the slaying of Rāvaṇa, is fulfilled in the Bālakāṇḍa.
It is said to be so;

the meaning is that it is expressed precisely by the mention of the victory over Bhārgava, who had himself conquered Rāvaṇa and Kārtavīrya. For the poet who composed [the work] after the *Bālacarita*, his "poetic composition" (*kavitā*) consists of the five cantos beginning with the *Ayodhyākāṇḍa*.
*Prakriyā* means *prakāra* (mode),
which is a particularity (*viśeṣa*), a particularity that differentiates a generality (*sāmānya*);
it is not [the same as] another [kind of particularity] because of the absence of the heaviness (*gaurava*) induced by that [latter].

That is to say, it is a cause for wonder; the sense is that while it is not surprising that he, who defeated the son of Bhṛgu (Paraśurāma) while still a child, should defeat Rāvaṇa as a youth, nevertheless—

The meaning is that he will satisfy the world because it is meritorious due to its description of the deeds of the Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa*). Regarding the reading *tattatkriyāgauravāt*— it refers to those various actions (*tāśca tāśca kriyāḥ*).

Although those various actions— such as the slaying of Vālin and the building of the bridge— have already been described for the most part, nevertheless, regarding those actions like the slaying of Vālin and the building of the bridge which are included within the totality of the means for the destruction of Rāvaṇa,
[he speaks] because of great respect arising from the fact that they require superhuman effort to accomplish.
"Quite another" means entirely new and truly wondrous; therefore, the meaning is that it alone brings satisfaction to the world. //146//
"Māṅgalika" means worthy of auspiciousness.
From this point until "they bow down" (309),
[the narrative] is established solely through Daśaratha's preparations for the consecration.
Because the king's sovereignty is stabilized by the present consecration, this is the constituent element (*aṅga*) called *kṛti*;
as it has been said: "Kṛti is the pacification of the object already attained" (310); here, *śamana* = [the act of calming].
The stabilization [of the meaning] is expressed by "tadehi" and so forth, and by the words "rājanvantaḥ. By this, he declares that Rāma is richly endowed with the qualities of a king. //147//
"High and low" means the consecrations of the ministers, the commander-in-chief, the domestic priest, and so forth;
"high and low" [is used] because of the irregular formation (nipātana) of the word *uccāvacākiñcana*.
Excellent!

(311) Regarding "five-limbed" (*pañcāṅga*): it refers to the chest, the cheeks, the chin, and the forehead. As it has been said: "The forehead, the chin, the two cheeks, and the chest—this is the five-limbed [prostration] used for saluting deities and others."
Thus it is proclaimed. (312) "Nāndīvādyāni" refers to auspicious musical instruments;
they are so called because the term *nāndī* is used figuratively in the sense of "auspiciousness.
[The phrase] begins with "udayad-udaya... and so forth.
In you, who possess the aggregate known as the eternally arisen Dharma, the neck indeed bears the burden by means of that very Dharma alone.
"The earth is supported"—this is the manner of instruction. "Seen and unseen" refers to those brought about by enemies. "Where indeed do they search?
means that they do not find them.

Furthermore, just as individual souls such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others receive the designation "Self" due to their similarity in the mere quality of consciousness, and perform the creation of the world and so forth— which is established by that mere act of seeing— themselves, although in reality...
Because there is no consciousness apart from that [Self], it is thus heard in scripture: "He who first creates Brahmā and who indeed imparts the Vedas to him" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.18). Likewise:

The meaning is that Indra and the others, possessing the title of world-protectors (dikpāla) merely by virtue of the sovereignty established at that particular time, are as if personally performing the protection of the world through your grace; for this very reason, they are mere sources of intimidation.
A "bibhīṣikā" is a figure made of grass and other materials representing a person or similar being;
for it indeed causes fear among deer and other animals in all directions, just like an actual person.
It protects the crops from them; likewise, the meaning is that they too, empowered by you, will protect the world from demons. //148//
Shame arises from revealing one's own greatness;
this refers to [the statement] "You alone are the primal person."
Because it brings about such a conviction (*sambhāvanā*), speech is indeed a constituent part [of the means of knowledge];
as it has been said: "And the attainment of authority (*āpti*) through the means of knowledge (*māna*)."

"Speech" (bhāṣaṇam), [referring to] "Laṅkā and so forth. "Puṣpaka" refers to that which is named Puṣpaka. "One" (ekām); Laṅkā is expressed here in the feminine gender, while "the other" (anyat) [is neuter].

The *puṣpaka*. This is the constituent element (*aṅga*) called *pūrvabhāva*, because it establishes the matter to be accomplished; as it has been said: "The sight of what is to be done and the attainment of the marvelous."
"In the embracing of the prior state. (315) //149//
"O Father, [your] command," and so forth.

By describing the command as the crest-jewel of his crown, and by characterizing that crown— consisting of the protection of deities and others remaining after the slaughter of the wicked Rāvaṇa— as the duty of a consecrated kṣatriya, namely the protection of subjects;
"It was said: 'From the perspective of worldly view, this forest-dwelling has been ordained by our father, but in reality, it is indeed the consecration.
Mahāpotrī is Ādivarāha; for him, the Vindhya mountain is his very tusk."
Because it is difficult of access; sporting there, she is a *śabarī* whose primary feature is leaves— that is, a *śabarī* possessing leafy coverings.
The compound is formed according to the *śākapārthiva* rule (Pāṇini 2.1.69).

Just as she was difficult for other men to behold, so too is the earth [difficult to traverse] due to the abundance of heroes; thus there is a similarity with Śabarī. By the phrase "at the end of the aeon" (*kalpānte*), he states that even during the dissolution of the world (*pralaya*), the bridge was not overwhelmed by water.
Marking the boundary— that is, dividing it—
the designation "southern" and "western" applies specifically to that very bridge over the ocean.

This is because it is perceived as such through contact with the eastern, northern, and southwestern [sides]. By the dual form "jalanidhī" (the two oceans), the vastness of the bridge is expressed, which produces the perception of multiplicity even though there is only one.
Regarding the word "nirmita" (constructed): it is because it is situated above like a raft; the construction of the bridge begins from the bottom.
It is indeed bound once it has been performed. Thus,
having described the three quarters and the incidental results consisting of the forms of phenomena known as the consecration, the ground, the mandala, and the inspection of the completion;
Now he states the primary fruit, called "the protection of the entire world," beginning with the words "And what has been done," etc. *Upasarga* means affliction (*bādha*).
Alternatively, the construction may be: "Even at the end of the eon (*kalpānta*), affliction is avoided"; of that—

Because there is no arising even in another form once liberation has been attained, this is the limb named *upasaṃhāra* (conclusion), consisting in the inclusion of the primary and secondary fruits; as it has been said: "The attainment of the fruit is *upasaṃhāra*. (318)
Attainment is the narration of attainment. //150//

"Samunmīlat" and so forth: by "makarandas"—that is, by the specific powers (*śakti*) of word and meaning—and by "rasas"; "upacinvantu" means "may they bring about. The sense is: "May the constant study of literature be accomplished. "Janaḥ" refers to the listener.

*Parimala* consists of the power (*śakti*) of the meanings of words such as *lakṣya* (the indicated) and *vyaṅgya* (the suggested). By the word "profound" (*gambhīra*), he expresses its capacity for critical investigation (*vimarśa*). He states that the refutation of those who do not engage in such investigation is a cause of suffering.
Likewise, praise is also [a form of commendation]; thus, there is the employment of words denoting qualities. //151//
"Of the god," and so forth.
*Vīrayaśorasāyana* is a medicinal elixir that brings about freedom from old age and death;
he is of that nature. *Madhusyanda* is a single flow of honey (*kṣaudra*). For generally...

In elixirs (*rasāyana*), there is an abundance of honey (*mākṣika*); even in the case of a medicinal herb, the word "honey" is used in the sense of "taste for the tongue. [The term] *śaṣkulī* is used because of its resemblance to that [shape].
The sense is that it is "immersed" and "that which is grasped. Sound is a quality (*guṇa*); for sound is indeed the quality of space (*ākāśa*).
For poets, "sound" means "poetry" (*kāvya*); for it is through poetry alone that fame is made stable. (319)
Thus, poetry possesses the nature of an elixir (*rasāyana*).
As it has been said: "The reflection of the glory of the first kings, having reached the mirror of literary composition..."
"Even in their absence, it does not perish of its own accord," (320)—
meaning, as long as the three streams persist.
The meaning is: "May it flourish for that long.
These two verses constitute the dramatic element known as *praśasti* (eulogy), because they consist of auspicious benedictions; as it has been said: "Praśasti..."
The proclamation of auspiciousness: (321) thus //152//
Thus ends the seventh act in the *Anargharāghava-pañcikā*, composed by Viṣṇu, the son of Muktinātha.
